news.Title: 「黃仁勳調查」衝擊南亞科！一度跌停 買在8月高點者一張已虧逾30萬元
news.Content:
美國加州檢察長邦塔（Rob Bonta）19日向美媒《POLITICO》證實，目前已對AI晶片大廠輝達（Nvidia）展開正式調查。受此利空消息重擊，記憶體大廠南亞科（2408）今日股價面臨沉重賣壓，盤中一度打入跌停價264.5元，買在八月高點者，帳面每張虧損30多萬元。隨後低接買盤隨即湧入承接，推升成交量迅速放大至近5萬張，跌停隨之打開；截至目前，股價維持在265元附近震盪整理，跌幅略為收斂至9%以上，分析師表示，先別急著進場接刀。

南亞科今日盤中最低下探至264.5元，一舉跌破5月20日低點265.5元，創下近5個月來新低。回顧8月28日波段高點569元，短短不到三個月時間，股價累計跌幅已超過五成；若投資人買在最高點且抱股至今，換算下來每張帳面虧損已超過30.4萬元。

倫元投顧分析師王春盛指出，AI運算高度依賴高頻寬記憶體（HBM），一旦輝達面臨調查甚至影響晶片出貨動能，連帶將波及上游記憶體的整體需求量。觀察南亞科今日盤中重摔至跌停價264.5元，再度改寫波段新低，顯示短線市場賣壓相當沉重。

不過，王春盛也強調，回歸基本面檢視，南亞科2026年第三季單季營收達1,336.49億元，季增61.9%，毛利率高達85.7%，單季每股純益（EPS）25.4元，累計前三季EPS更達49.28元，整體獲利表現依舊亮眼。

在技術面與操作策略上，王春盛分析，目前南亞科KD指標已落入超賣區，股價跌深後確實具備醞釀技術性反彈的條件，但「超賣並不代表立即止跌」。建議手中仍持有股票的投資人不宜貿然向下攤平，應先密切觀察跌停打開後的籌碼換手與成交量能變化；至於空手者，則建議耐心等待明確止跌訊號浮現、股價重新站回短期均線後再行分批布局，切忌急著進場接刀。

輝達前執行長黃仁勳與疑似具備中國大陸間諜身分的黃樂（Alice Huang）婚外情，美國加州檢察長已展開正式調查，預計要釐清輝達的先進晶片或核心機密資訊是否因此流入中國大陸，以及該公司在相關資訊揭露上是否涉有誤導投資人與公眾之嫌。

news.Title: History Says This Brilliant ETF Could Help You Turn $500 Per Month Into $784,100 While Barely Lifting a Finger.
news.Content:
Hitting it big in the stock market doesn't have to mean getting in early on the next Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) or Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL). Of course, that would be appreciated, but it's far from required to make good money in the market. Countless investors have built wealth by leaning on broad ETFs and trusting the power of time and consistency.

One ETF that can be a great addition to your portfolio is the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (NYSEMKT:VUG). It has been a consistent market beater, and based on its historical returns, $500 monthly investments could grow to over $784,100 in 25 years.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Growth and stability are a win-win

VUG is the best of both worlds. On one side, its growth focus offers strong upside. On the other hand, because it holds only large-cap growth stocks , it offers a bit more stability than smaller growth stocks typically do.

A small growth stock might struggle to survive a major economic downturn. I don't question whether companies like Apple, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), and Eli Lilly (NYSE:LLY) can. Here are VUG's top 10 holdings:

Apple: 13.69%

Nvidia: 12.78%

Microsoft: 10.49%

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Class A: 4.44%

Amazon: 4.35%

Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO): 4.26%

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META): 3.80%

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) Class C: 3.53%

Eli Lilly: 3.37%

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA): 3.16%

VUG is tech-heavy (72.1%) because that's where much of the market's growth has been over the past couple of decades, but it also has decent non-tech exposure that provides some hedge. Just outside VUG's top 10 holdings are industry leaders like Visa (NYSE:V) and Costco (NASDAQ:COST), which have performed well for investors over the years.

Some have worried that major tech valuations have become inflated amid the current AI boom, increasing the chance of a pullback or correction. While those concerns may be warranted, they don't diminish the tech sector's growth potential or the companies leading the way for VUG.

Plenty of tech trends -- whether it's AI, cloud computing, or cybersecurity -- are on the earlier end of what many expect them to become. Investing in VUG is about capitalizing on growth while having a little crutch from other industries.

The math behind $772,200

Since it began trading in January 2004, VUG has averaged an annual total return of 11.9%. Past results don't guarantee future performance, but if we assume it continues averaging those returns, here's how much $500 monthly investments could grow to in different numbers of years:

How much you ultimately make will depend on time and returns (which we can't predict), but the bigger takeaway is how powerful time can be in investing. In each case, you would've contributed much less than your ending investment.

VUG has a lot of overlap at the top with popular indexes like the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC), so if you're investing in an S&P 500 ETF or Nasdaq-100 ETF, double-check that you're not too concentrated in VUG's top holdings.

Apple, Nvidia, and Microsoft are great companies, no doubt, but part of the reason for investing in ETFs is diversification. There's no need to override that by overexposing to the same handful of stocks.

news.Title: 1 Unstoppable Stock to Buy Before It Joins NVDA and AAPL in the $1 Trillion Club
news.Content:
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) briefly became a $1 trillion company in September, but it lost that milestone after a prolonged artificial intelligence (AI) stock correction. However, the chipmaker is set to rejoin Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) as a trillion-dollar company. These are the catalysts that can drive the stock higher.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nvidia confusion creates an opening

AMD has been viewed as the No. 2 graphics processing unit (GPU) chipmaker for several years, with Nvidia comfortably holding on to the top spot. However, Nvidia suddenly faces significant uncertainty with former CEO Jensen Huang out of the company and angling for a comeback.

Nvidia currently doesn't seem receptive to a reunion, and that can cost the company. Some investors argue that Huang's departure will make it difficult for Nvidia to continue innovating despite the competitive edge it has already obtained.

The AI industry is moving rapidly, and leadership complexities can cost Nvidia valuable time. It can be the difference between missing out on the latest technology and watching hyperscalers turn to alternatives.

This scenario positions AMD as the chipmaker with the most to gain from the confusion, and the company has been taking major steps to close the gap. For instance, AMD is making its chip fleet more attractive by making it much easier for developers to port existing Nvidia CUDA applications to its HIP platform.

Nvidia's CUDA was previously a major moat. Moving to another software essentially meant rewriting vast amounts of code, but that's no longer the case. If AMD can win over more businesses with an easier migration, it creates more headaches for a company already full of them.

Growth was picking up before the Nvidia shake-up

Although Nvidia has captured most of the headlines throughout the AI boom, AMD has been quietly accelerating its growth. Data center revenue surged by 97% year over year in the third quarter, while overall revenue reached $13.4 billion, up by 45% year over year. That also represents a 16% sequential boost.

AMD CEO Lisa Su told investors that demand for its AI products is still accelerating. The chipmaker also remains confident that revenue growth will surge in the coming years, along with higher net profit margins.

Story Continues

AMD trades at a 30 forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which may be higher than what some investors are willing to handle. However, this same company almost doubled its net income year over year. AMD wrapped up the quarter with an 18.2% net profit margin, and if it can get closer to Nvidia's 62% net profit margin, the stock should have an easy time reclaiming a $1 trillion market cap and marching toward new highs.

news.Title: HSBC Just Turned Bullish on Cisco Stock Again. Here’s Why It Expects 40% Upside.
news.Content:
Cisco Systems (CSCO) has long worn the label of a mature networking giant, rarely linked to rapid growth. Yet now, the company is shaking up Wall Street's expectations. Fueled by a wave of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investment, strong enterprise demand, and an exceptional quarter, Cisco has prompted HSBC to abandon its cautious stance, upgrade the stock to "Buy," and raise its price target to $133.

With the bank forecasting nearly 40% upside, Cisco's growth revival is quickly becoming impossible to ignore. Let's take a closer look.

Stop Missing Market Moves: Get the FREE Barchart Brief – your midday dose of stock movers, trending sectors, and actionable trade ideas, delivered right to your inbox. Sign Up Now!

HSBC's Change of Heart Has a Clear Catalyst

On Nov. 17, HSBC raised CSCO stock to "Buy" from "Hold" and increased its price target to $133 from $120. The new target implies approximately 40% potential upside from current levels. The move is notable because HSBC had downgraded Cisco stock from "Buy" to "Hold" in August, cutting its target from $137 to $120. Its latest upgrade reverses that decision, driven by a stronger networking outlook, firmer AI-related demand, and a valuation it considers attractive relative to growth.

HSBC expects Cisco's networking revenue to compound at 19.2% annually from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2029. The firm also forecasts adjusted EPS to grow 14.9% annually from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2031. The $133 price target applies a 23 times multiple to the estimated next-12-month adjusted EPS of $5.78. In other words, the valuation depends on earnings growth continuing and investors maintaining that earnings multiple.

The Quarter Was Strong Because Demand Reached Beyond AI

Cisco's first quarter of fiscal 2027 performance encouraged HSBC to shift from caution to a more optimistic stance. The company reported $18.5 billion in revenue, up 24% year-over-year (YOY). Adjusted EPS rose 40% YOY to $1.40, while adjusted operating margin reached 37.8%. CFO Mark Patterson said the company exceeded the high end of its guidance for revenue, operating margin, and EPS. Cisco focused not just on shipping more equipment but on turning the stronger quarter into higher profitability.

Story Continues

Product revenue rose 32% YOY to $14.7 billion, while services revenue grew just 1% to $3.9 billion. Networking stole the spotlight with a remarkable 43% increase, while security, collaboration, and software each posted steady gains of 7%, 8%, and 8%, respectively, with software reaching $6.1 billion. Clearly, hardware drove this acceleration, not services.

Orders provide an important check on revenue momentum. Product orders climbed 21%, backed by double-digit growth across every region. Service provider and cloud orders soared 47%, while enterprise and public-sector orders advanced 15% and 13%. Networking orders surged 28%, marking its ninth-straight quarter of double-digit gains. This broad-based recovery reduces reliance on hyperscalers.

The order picture also extends into traditional networking. Campus networking orders increased 14%, and telecom orders rose 20%. Cisco is benefiting not only from new AI data centers but also from customers upgrading enterprise networks and connectivity. These projects can broaden the addressable demand pool and make the growth profile less dependent on the timing of a few large AI deployments.

Nonetheless, hyperscalers still remain the biggest growth catalyst. Cisco projects $9 billion in AI infrastructure sales to these customers in fiscal 2027, up from about $4 billion in fiscal 2026 and higher than its earlier $7.5 billion forecast. Management pointed to stronger orders, better visibility, and three AI design wins with Silicon One systems and 1.6-terabit optics.

Cisco ended the quarter with $46.2 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO), up 8% YOY, and annual recurring revenue (ARR) of $32.7 billion, up 4%. Subscription revenue accounted for 44% of sales. No doubt, there is a sharp gap between hardware and services growth, but these numbers also reflect a steadier revenue foundation as networking equipment demand moves through its cycle.

Upbeat Outlook Adds to the Bullish Case

Cisco raised its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $74.8 billion to $75.8 billion and adjusted EPS to $5.47 to $5.53. The revenue midpoint implies roughly 19% YOY growth. For Q2, management expects revenue of $18 billion to $18.2 billion and EPS of $1.34 to $1.36.

Yet the quarter revealed a price to pay. Adjusted gross margin edged down to 65.6%, and product gross margin slipped to 63.7%. Management pointed to a heavier hardware mix and rising memory costs, with some relief from productivity gains and pricing. The very products fueling growth are, for now, less profitable than those they are replacing. Management remains confident it will reach a 36% adjusted operating margin for fiscal 2027, up from 34.8% in fiscal 2026, suggesting productivity and scale gains could help offset mounting pressures.

Operating cash flow surged 36% to $4.4 billion, highlighting strong financial momentum. Now, all eyes are on whether rising memory and component costs will persist as hardware claims a bigger slice of sales. Cisco returned $3.7 billion to shareholders during the quarter through dividends and share buybacks, showing its capacity to generate strong cash flow while fueling growth and rewarding investors.

The $9 Billion AI Opportunity Is Not Free of Its Costs

Cisco's AI forecast depends on customers deploying systems on schedule. Management flagged optics supply as a potential constraint, while the second half of the year will test the company with tougher benchmarks. Delayed hyperscaler projects could shift revenue between quarters, and lower gross margins may limit how much sales growth reaches earnings. These risks lurk behind that bullish forecast.

Basically, HSBC is betting networking growth isn't a one-quarter spike. Its 19.2% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) forecast and $133 price target rest on the belief that AI infrastructure and broader networking demand will keep powering ahead. While some analysts have cut their price targets, they have also acknowledged the strong results and retained bullish ratings.

Cisco Must Prove It Can Keep Growth on Track

Cisco's story extends far beyond the $9 billion AI forecast. Surging networking revenue, strong orders from diverse customers, and rising guidance fuel its growth engine. The challenge is turning this demand into profitable sales while managing component costs and supply constraints. The next quarters will reveal whether Cisco can turn orders into deliveries, stabilize margins, and meet its ambitious EPS targets. If the company delivers, CSCO stock can hit HSBC's bullish target of $133 or even the Street's high price estimate of $150.

Overall, Cisco stock holds a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating on Wall Street. Of the 26 analysts covering the stock, 16 have a "Strong Buy," one has a "Moderate Buy," and nine have a "Hold" rating. The average price target sits at $129.65, suggesting a possible 37% climb, while the most bullish estimate of $150 implies potential upside of 58% from current levels.

news.Title: Nvidia vs. Intel: One AI Stock Is Worth the Drama, the Other Isn’t Worth the Wait, Says Investor
news.Content:
For a while, the only thing Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) and Intel ( NASDAQ:INTC ) had in common was that they both made chips.

Nvidia rode the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies, while Intel spent years trying to repair its business. Now they share a problem: shareholders who aren't sure what comes next. Nvidia released its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, its first since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, and the stock still fell the next day. Intel's slide deepened after it issued a weak outlook in late October.

Nvidia's revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion, and interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%. On the same call, though, board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. That came only hours after Huang said he would be honored to return.

Nvidia stock now hovers near its lowest level since around June 2025. This week Intel was hit by a shareholder lawsuit and by a filing showing that Nvidia sold about a quarter of its Intel stake. Intel shares sit about 60% below their June peak.

So, where to now for these two embattled chip giants?

An investor going by the moniker of The Curious Analyst (TCA) has two very different reads on these stocks.

On Nvidia, TCA thinks the leadership drama is already reflected in the share price. The stock fell sharply when Huang stepped down, but the board's refusal to bring him back drew a much milder reaction. The investor takes that as a sign the market trusts Kress. In TCA's view, investors can now see what Nvidia looks like without its founder, and the danger of relying on one person has faded.

The business case rests on the product cycle. Vera Rubin added nearly $20 billion in revenue from the previous quarter, and the investor expects growth to hold up as it ramps alongside Blackwell Ultra. TCA also expects Nvidia to use up its remaining buyback authorization of about $227 billion by the end of fiscal 2028, as management has said it will, which would shrink the share count. Assuming a net margin of about 50%, TCA's fiscal 2028 EPS estimate lands at $16.12.

Nvidia trades at roughly 10 times forward earnings, far below its historical range. TCA thinks a multiple in the low 20s, near the sector median, would be reasonable. The investor also sees an upside that the model leaves out for now. SpaceX caught Starship's upper stage for the first time last weekend, and TCA thinks cheaper launches could eventually create demand for AI hardware and data centers in space.

Story Continues

The main risks are a slowdown in AI spending and the chance that investors won't pay a higher multiple without Huang. Still, TCA notes that Nvidia impressed the market in the middle of an AI selloff and a leadership crisis, and sees that as evidence the company is on solid ground.

Bottom line, TCA reiterated a Strong Buy rating on NVDA stock. (To watch The Curious Analyst's track record, click here )

The investor is far less comfortable with Intel. Its fourth-quarter revenue guidance midpoint of $15.5 billion fell well short of the roughly $17 billion analysts expected, and the stock lost more than a quarter of its value the next day. For TCA, the bigger problem is profitability. Intel's trailing 12-month net margin is about -20%, and right now the market has little patience for cash burn.

TCA's model assumes revenue grows about 9% next year and allows for a recovery to a 6% net margin, roughly the sector median. That gives a 2027 EPS estimate of $0.78, less than half the Wall Street consensus of $1.79. The one thing TCA finds encouraging is Intel's long-term earnings growth outlook. Even so, Intel trades at about three times Nvidia's forward multiple.

The risks are more dilution after a stock sale of more than $20 billion in August, margins that could slip again, and a multiple investors may stop paying.

While TCA is no fan of the stock right now, the investor stops short of rating it a Sell. TCA argues that the post-earnings collapse already made shareholders pay for one disappointing quarter, and Intel still has a real role in PCs, data centers and AI. It has come back from tough stretches before. The investor wants to see fourth-quarter results and the 2027 outlook before deciding which way to go.

For now, TCA rates INTC stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral).

On the Street, NVDA claims a Moderate Buy consensus rating, while its $232.59 average price target points to 12-month returns of 54%. INTC is rated a Hold, although, interestingly, its $90.93 average target suggests shares will gain 66% over the one-year timeframe. (See NVDA stock forecast or INTC stock forecast )

news.Title: Apple Nears a Rare Long-Term DRAM Supply Deal With Samsung Electronics. What This Means for AAPL Stock.
news.Content:
The iPhone is selling faster, but the memory inside it is getting more expensive. Apple (AAPL) reported $57.6 billion in iPhone revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter, up 17% from a year earlier. Yet after stripping out the benefit of tariff refunds — about $2.2 billion — its gross margin fell from the prior quarter, largely because of higher memory costs.

Apple expects a gross margin of 45% to 46% in the December quarter, with higher memory costs among the factors weighing on that outlook. That makes the reported talks with Samsung Electronics over a rare deal to secure DRAM supply for several years especially timely.

More News from Barchart

Dear SpaceX Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 19

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 20

$1.6 Billion Loss: Billionaire Bill Ackman Says He Was 'A Little Bit Surprised' by Berkshire's $10 Billion Alphabet Bet, 'They Got It at a 6% Discount, But So What?'

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

Would securing more memory give Wall Street a reason to raise its earnings expectations for Apple, or would it simply help the company meet them? Let's take a closer look.

What a Samsung Deal Would Secure

Apple designs and sells iPhones, iPads, Macs, and wearables, and offers services such as iCloud, Apple Music, and Apple Pay. The company's iPhones, iPads, and Macs use dynamic random access memory (DRAM) to temporarily store the data apps need while they run.

The company is reportedly close to signing a rare multiyear deal with Samsung Electronics to secure a minimum supply of those chips. This deal would run for four to five years, starting in the first half of 2027, a departure from Apple's usual shorter contracts. Samsung would commit to supplying a minimum volume, although it is unclear how many chips that would cover. The timing helps explain why Apple is willing to commit for several years.

TrendForce, a technology market research firm, expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise 10% to 15% from the previous quarter in the final three months of 2026. That forecast reflects industry pricing rather than Apple's own costs. Meanwhile, SK Hynix (SKHY) says long-term agreements already cover more than half of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028.

The deal could help Apple keep iPhones and MacBooks in production as suppliers shift capacity toward artificial intelligence (AI) servers. It could also support the foldable iPhone Duo as Apple ramps production, although Apple hasn't identified memory as the cause of that device's supply constraints.

Story Continues

Apple's clearest potential benefit is a lower risk of lost sales from memory shortages. The catch is that securing enough chips to fill orders wouldn't protect Apple's margins if memory prices keep rising.

Where AAPL Stands Financially

Apple reported Q4 fiscal 2026 results on Nov. 2, with revenue rising 12% year-over-year (YOY) to $114.5 billion, beating the $113.6 billion consensus estimate. Its EPS of $2.10 also beat the $1.99 estimate, while gross and operating margins held steady YOY at 47.9% and 31.1%, respectively.

Apple's product revenue rose 12% to $82.9 billion, led by iPhone sales climbing 17% to $57.6 billion on strong iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro demand. Its active iPhone base hit a record, with record upgrades in the United States, China, India, and Japan.

Mac revenue rose 24% to $10.8 billion, driven by MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro demand, with room to attract first-time buyers and upgraders in emerging markets. Services revenue grew 10% YOY to $31.6 billion, supported by strength in cloud, payments, advertising, video, and music, more than 2.5 billion active devices, and more than 1.5 billion paid subscriptions.

AAPL stock fell after earnings but closed on Nov. 18 at $352.45 per share. The stock is up 29% year-to-date (YTD) and up 30% over 52 weeks.

Apple's market capitalization stands at $5.12 trillion, with a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple and a forward P/E ratio of 39.9 times and 37.2 times, respectively, versus sector medians of about 27 times and 26 times. The forward annual dividend of $1.08 per share yields 0.31%.

CEO John Ternus flagged supply constraints and rising memory costs. The December quarter gross margin outlook of 45% to 46% reflects those higher costs and the initial Siri AI rollout expenses, per CFO Kevan Parekh. Apple sees room to expand iCloud+ and paid subscriptions, with new AI features offering another potential source of revenue.

What Analysts Expect From Apple

Wall Street expects Apple to earn $2.94 per share in the December quarter, up 3.5% from $2.84 a year earlier. Apple is expected to report those results on Feb. 4, 2027.

Analyst Dan Ives thinks investors should buy the dip. Ives argues Apple doesn't need to build data centers on the same scale as its rivals to bring AI features to the iPhone. It can lean on suppliers and cloud partners instead. He also thinks investors are underestimating how many customers will upgrade to the iPhone Duo.

Not everyone is willing to pay up for that story. Morgan Stanley rates AAPL stock as "Overweight," but its $350 price target is already below current levels. KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel is more skeptical. Nispel rates Apple as "Underweight" with a $250 target, citing the risk of slowing hardware sales.

That gap between ratings and price targets extends beyond those two firms. Apple has a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating from 41 analysts, yet the average target of $344.69 is about 2% below the current price of AAPL stock.

Conclusion

Apple's reported deal with Samsung would help keep iPhones shipping even if memory gets harder to buy. But with prices still tied to the market, securing chips won't shield Apple from higher costs. The most likely outcome is fewer supply headaches rather than a meaningful bump in earnings. That makes the deal good news for Apple's business, but probably not enough to lift AAPL on its own, especially with shares already trading above Wall Street's average price target.

news.Title: This Is Incredible News for AMD Stock Investors (Hint: It’s Bad News for Intel)
news.Content:
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) has been crushing Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) in the central processing unit (CPU) market, which explains why the former has been enjoying significantly stronger growth in recent quarters.

In fact, AMD is all set to become a bigger company than Intel in terms of revenue in the current quarter, and a closer look at the developments in the CPU market will tell us just why that's the case. Mercury Research, which provides data on the CPU market, recently released its third-quarter findings, which point to further gains for AMD in a lucrative space.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's take a closer look.

Image source: AMD.

AMD is becoming bigger in server CPUs

Server CPU demand has been increasing phenomenally owing to the growth in inference and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workloads in data centers. Counterpoint Research points out that the ratio of GPU (graphics processing unit) to CPU in AI data centers has moved from 4:1 to 2:1. What's more, the firm sees a GPU to CPU ratio of 1:1 amid rising demand for agentic AI.

In simpler terms, AI data centers are now using more CPUs per GPU, leading to a phenomenal increase in the total addressable market (TAM) for server CPUs. AMD predicts that server CPU TAM will hit $220 billion in 2030, clocking annual growth of more than 50% through the end of the decade. So, AMD's rising share in this space is good news for investors.

Mercury Research points out that AMD's server CPU market share increased to 35.5% in the third quarter, a significant improvement over the year-ago period's reading of 27.8%. So, Intel lost significant ground in this market, which explains why the growth of its data center and AI (DCAI) segment was much slower than AMD's in Q3.

While AMD posted a 97% year-over-year increase in data center revenue last quarter, Intel reported a 78% increase in this segment. The gap is poised to widen in the current quarter. That's because AMD is anticipating 66% revenue growth in the current quarter to $17 billion. Intel, on the other hand, expects 13% revenue growth in the current quarter to $15.5 billion, at the midpoint of its guidance range. That's slower than the 21% revenue jump Intel delivered in Q3.

AMD can continue hurting Intel in this market

It won't be surprising to see AMD taking more market share from Intel in server CPUs next year, thanks mainly to its sixth-generation server CPUs, codenamed Venice. The company began shipping Venice processors to customers last quarter and expects a significant sales ramp next year. In the words of AMD CEO Lisa Su:

Story Continues

We began revenue shipments of EPYC Venice processors in the third quarter, and the first OEM systems are on track for availability this quarter. Early demand is the strongest we have seen for any new EPYC generation.

Our OEM and ODM partners have committed more than 240 Venice platforms, 20% more than Turin, and cloud providers are deploying Venice this quarter ahead of instance rollouts planned for early 2027.

AMD has also launched a server rack system, known as Helion, equipped with only Venice CPUs. The company points out that Helion will be offered by every major server original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and original device manufacturer (ODM) for running inference, agentic, and superintelligence workloads in the cloud

In all, Su believes that the Venice CPUs are "positioning us to gain share and significantly grow our server business." As such, I won't be surprised to see AMD's server CPU revenue jumping nicely over the next five years, driven mainly by market share gains. For instance, if AMD captures even half of the server CPU TAM in 2030, it can generate $110 billion in revenue from this segment alone (based on the $220 billion TAM estimate).

That implies a big jump in AMD's top line after four years, considering that it has generated $45 billion in revenue over the trailing twelve months. Intel, on the other hand, may continue to struggle in server CPUs and fail to keep up with AMD's rapidly improving growth trajectory. As a result, buying AMD stock over Intel seems like the logical thing to do right now, as it trades at a cheaper 31 times forward earnings compared to Chipzilla's forward price-to-earnings ratio of 32.3.

news.Title: Trump Just Disclosed Tesla and SpaceX Stock Purchases. Here's What His Portfolio Moves Reveal
news.Content:
President Donald Trump's latest stock transactions are out, and yes, Tesla and SpaceX made the list.

On Thursday, the Office of Government Ethics made public a 25-page transaction report covering hundreds of transactions from September. It shows purchases of Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) stock, along with sales of household names like McDonald's (NYSE:MCD) and Home Depot (NYSE:HD).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

So how have the moves panned out, and what do they say about the billionaire president's portfolio? So far, the results are mixed: Several of the stocks Trump sold have outperformed the Tesla and SpaceX shares he bought, and the filing seems to indicate a shift toward dividends and bonds rather than a big bet on Elon Musk.

The Tesla and SpaceX buys were small

Reports like this one list each trade as a dollar range rather than an exact amount. Trump's four Tesla purchases, made between Sept. 1 and Sept. 10, total between $117,004 and $330,000. His two SpaceX stock purchases add up to $16,002 to $65,000. He also bought $100,001 to $250,000 in SpaceX bonds that pay 5.35% interest and mature in 2031.

The president also had much bigger moves in the filing. On Sept. 23 alone, Trump sold shares of McDonald's, Home Depot, Comcast (NASDAQ:CMCSA) and Fidelity National Information Services (NYSE:FIS) worth $1,000,001 to $5 million apiece. He also sold Nike (NYSE:NKE) and Constellation Brands (NYSE:STZ) stock worth $500,001 to $1 million each. The single largest transaction in the report, made the same day, was a purchase of $5,000,001 to $25 million of the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (NYSEMKT:VIG).

The scorecard so far

Here's how each has done since the day of the transaction, based on that day's closing price and Thursday afternoon trading, according to Nasdaq data. The filing doesn't give the exact prices Trump paid or received.

The buys:

Tesla: up about 6% since Sept. 1, the day of its largest purchase

SpaceX: down about 7% since Sept. 24, the day of its largest purchase

Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF: up about 2% since Sept. 23

The Sept. 23 sales:

Constellation Brands: up 21%

McDonald's: up 14%

Home Depot: up 13%

Comcast: up 10%

Nike: down 5%

Fidelity National Information Services: down 25%

Four of the six big stocks Trump sold have climbed 10% or more since then. But the FIS sale dodged a 25% drop, marking the best call in the batch. In other words, it's a mixed record, like most investors', and of course, these are just short-term movements. Long-term the picture can look vastly different.

Story Continues

Why copying a politician's trades is harder than it looks

There are three big problems with treating this filing as a stock-picking guide.

The first is timing. These transactions happened in September and became public about eight weeks later. Anyone who copied the McDonald's and Home Depot sales on Thursday would be selling after those stocks had already rallied.

The second is size. Because transactions are reported in ranges, a $1,001 Tesla purchase and a $15,000 one look identical. It's hard to tell a big bet from routine housekeeping.

The third is motive. The filing doesn't say who chose these transactions or why. Many of them involve funds and municipal bonds, which make the account look more like a rebalancing portfolio than a series of handpicked bets.

What investors should take away

Tesla and SpaceX are two of the most talked-about tech stocks on the market, and a presidential purchase makes a fun headline. But the biggest message in Trump's filing is a lesson in diversification: a large move into a dividend fund, trims to individual stocks, and lots of bonds.

If you like Tesla or SpaceX, buy them because you believe in the businesses and can hold through the swings, not because they showed up on a government disclosure form.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Continue »

Jonathan Ponciano has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool recommends Comcast and Constellation Brands and recommends the following options: long January 2028 $320 calls on McDonald's and short January 2028 $340 calls on McDonald's. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy .

news.Title: Down More Than 40% in the Past Month, Here’s How You Should Play Sandisk Stock
news.Content:
Sandisk (SNDK) has been one of the most dramatic winners in the AI-driven memory boom this year, but the stock has now entered a sharp correction. Shares have fallen 43.8% over the past month, extending a selloff that has erased a significant portion of the gains built earlier this year. The latest weakness comes despite the company reporting a record fiscal first quarter and issuing stronger-than-expected guidance for the current quarter.

The pullback reflects growing concerns about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending, elevated NAND flash prices, and the possibility that memory demand could cool after a massive run. Sandisk has also been caught in the broader AI-stock selloff, with concerns surrounding Nvidia (NVDA) and data center spending weighing on memory and storage stocks. Moreover, investors are reassessing whether Sandisk's exceptionally strong margins and earnings growth can be sustained.

More News from Barchart

Dear SpaceX Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 19

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 20

$1.6 Billion Loss: Billionaire Bill Ackman Says He Was 'A Little Bit Surprised' by Berkshire's $10 Billion Alphabet Bet, 'They Got It at a 6% Discount, But So What?'

Get exclusive insights with the FREE Barchart Brief newsletter. Subscribe now for quick, incisive midday market analysis you won't find anywhere else.

With SNDK stock now sharply below its recent peak, is the recent plunge creating an attractive entry point, or is it signaling that Sandisk's AI-driven growth story has become too dependent on peak memory pricing?

About Sandisk Stock

Sandisk is a leading data storage and flash memory company headquartered in Milpitas, California. The company designs, develops, and manufactures a broad portfolio of NAND flash storage products, including solid-state drives (SSDs), memory cards, USB flash drives, and embedded storage solutions. The company's market cap has expanded dramatically, with its current standing at $110.5 billion.

Sandisk has delivered extraordinary returns over the past year, but the stock has recently undergone a brutal reversal. Shares are up 213% over the past 52 weeks and 225% year-to-date (YTD), reflecting the explosive investor enthusiasm surrounding the company's exposure to the AI-driven surge in data center storage and NAND flash demand.

However, that momentum has broken sharply. Sandisk stock has slumped 44.3% over the past six months and is now 67% below its 52-week peak, highlighting the severity of the recent correction.

Story Continues

The selloff has been driven less by a deterioration in Sandisk's near-term fundamentals and more by mounting concerns over the sustainability of elevated NAND prices, the potential for a 2027 memory glut, and broader doubts about the pace of AI infrastructure spending.

GF Securities recently warned that NAND oversupply could emerge next year as supply growth accelerates while consumer electronics demand weakens. As a pure-play NAND company, Sandisk is particularly exposed to any deterioration in memory pricing.

Moreover, the stock has also been caught in a broader semiconductor selloff, while concerns over AI spending, regulatory uncertainty surrounding data center construction, and weakness across memory peers have amplified the pressure on SNDK.

Notably, amid this pullback, the company is completing an 8-for-1 forward stock split after the market closes today, Nov. 19, with shares set to begin trading on a split-adjusted basis (at roughly one-eighth of the pre-split price) at the market open on Friday, Nov. 20.

SNDK stock is currently trading at a discount compared to the sector median, at 6.22 times sales and 3.92 times earnings.

Robust Q1 Financial Performance

Sandisk reported its fiscal first-quarter 2027 results on Oct. 29, for the quarter ended Oct. 2. Revenue jumped 378% year-over-year (YoY) to $11 billion. The growth was broad across the company's end markets, although data center demand was the standout.

Data center revenue surged to $4.8 billion from $269 million a year earlier, while Edge revenue climbed 320% to $5.8 billion from $1.4 billion. Consumer revenue, however, declined 39% to $397 million from $652 million, showing that the current growth story is being driven overwhelmingly by enterprise and AI-related storage rather than consumer demand.

Profitability improved even more dramatically as non-GAAP gross margin increased to 85.1% from 29.9%. Its operating expenses rose 17% to $598 million, while operating income jumped to $8.8 billion.

Its non-GAAP net income surged to $7.6 billion from $181 million, and non-GAAP EPS increased to $49.51 from $1.22, ahead of expectations. The magnitude of the improvement underscores how dramatically the company's earnings profile has changed as memory pricing and AI-driven storage demand have strengthened.

Cash generation was another major positive. Operating cash flow jumped to $6.4 billion from $488 million, while free cash flow increased to $6.3 billion from $438 million. Sandisk also returned $5 billion to shareholders through share repurchases during the quarter, buying back approximately 3.2 million shares.

Furthermore, management issued another strong outlook for fiscal Q2 2027, calling for revenue of $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion. The company expects non-GAAP gross margin to be 84.5% to 85.5%. Non-GAAP EPS is expected at $55 to $57 on a pre-split basis. Management also expects non-GAAP operating expenses of $540 million to $560 million.

Analysts remain optimistic, forecasting EPS of $226.01 for fiscal 2027, a substantial 225.7% YoY jump, followed by a further 26% rise to $284.86 in 2028.

What Do Analysts Expect for SNDK Stock?

Most recently, Bernstein analyst Mark Newman maintained a "Buy" rating and a $3,000 price target on SNDK, reiterating his bullish long-term view despite the stock's recent sharp pullback.

Furthermore, Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore maintained an "Overweight" rating and a $1,750 price target on Sandisk following its fiscal Q1 results.

Overall, SNDK stock has a consensus "Strong Buy" rating. Of the 25 analysts covering it, 19 advise a "Strong Buy," one suggests a "Moderate Buy," and the remaining five analysts are on the sidelines, giving it a "Hold" rating.

SNDK's average analyst price target of $2,039.38 indicates an upside of 164%, while Bernstein's Street-high target price of $3,000 indicates that the stock could rally as much as 289%.

The analysts boosted the technology company's ranking, owing to its R&D spend rising 32% from a fiscal year ago.

Apple rises to No. 30

Published with TheStreet , The Roundtable 100 ranks the top 100 publicly traded technology growth assets. Each is scored from 0 to 100 by the analysts of the Blue Ribbon Committee on five variables, Team, Safety, Value, Innovation, and Market Dominance, with the average forming the asset's Power Ranking. The list refreshes every Friday after the U.S. market close.

The Blue Ribbon Committee's analysts rank a company on the basis of its potential to grow in the future, not its current dominance.

Committee member John Slazas , who is the founder of the trading platform MKT.TRADE , made the amendment that lifted Apple's Innovation score from 36 to 76.

He wrote the earlier grade "says something different: that Apple has stopped building. The full-year results published November 2 and the annual report filed November 3 say the opposite."

Slazas pointed to the iPhone maker's R&D surging 32% from a year ago to $45.8 billion in fiscal 2026 — the highest spend ever.

The RTB 100 analyst also highlighted that the company's revenue rose 15% to a record $478.8 billion.

Follow Apple on the Roundtable 100

But the Blue Ribbon Committee fell short of granting the company an Innovation score of 80 as the analysts await new products.

"The target is 76, not the 80 baseline, until the new products show up in a full year of sales," Slazas said.

Apple also enjoys high scores on Team and Safety, its overall RTB 100 score being 75.

In the Nov. 13 ranking, Apple rose from No. 39 to No. 30.

news.Title: Apple’s head of iPhone camera software retires after eight years - Bloomberg
news.Content:
Investing.com -- Apple Inc's (NASDAQ:AAPL) vice president overseeing camera and photo software has retired, marking a rare leadership transition for a core engineering group behind the iPhone's primary consumer upgrade driver, according to Bloomberg. Jon McCormack stepped down at the end of October following an eight-year tenure leading development for the Camera and Photos applications and their underlying image-processing architecture.

Rather than appointing a direct successor to McCormack's vice president role, Apple is distributing his former responsibilities among existing deputies reporting to other executives, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. The restructuring places senior vice president of software engineering Craig Federighi in charge of managing the transition across a specialized division that bridges software algorithms, custom silicon, and optical hardware.

Camera performance remains a central pillar of Apple's hardware marketing and customer retention strategy, with iPhone users capturing trillions of photographs annually. Under McCormack's oversight, the software engineering teams delivered the redesigned selfie camera system for the iPhone 17 lineup and the customizable, professional-grade Camera interface alongside variable-aperture support on the iPhone 18 Pro models.

The leadership change arrives as smartphone photography undergoes a strategic shift toward generative artificial intelligence. Rivals including Alphabet Inc.'s Google and Samsung Electronics Co. have aggressively integrated generative tools capable of substantially altering captured images, challenging traditional definitions of photographic authenticity.

Internally, McCormack opposed using generative AI to fabricate or heavily manipulate photographs, favoring a philosophy centered on preserving real-world moments, according to Bloomberg's sources. While that stance contrasted with Apple's broader push to accelerate AI-powered software capabilities across its ecosystem, people familiar with the move indicated his retirement was not prompted by a dispute over corporate AI strategy.

news.Title: TSMC and Samsung's China Chip Pause Has Stakes Beyond AI
news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( NYSE:TSM ) and Samsung Electronics ( SSNLF ) have paused some chip shipments to China as they seek new U.S. export licenses, the Financial Times reported. The immediate concern for investors is that the restrictions reach beyond AI processors. They could also delay shipments of advanced smartphone chips and disrupt production schedules for Chinese handset makers.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 4 Warning Signs with KUASF.

Is TSM fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The new rules, which took effect Thursday, narrow the options for Chinese companies that design their own chips and rely on overseas manufacturers to make them. Some designers had used independent packaging and testing companies to verify that their products fell outside U.S. export controls. That route is now closed for affected shipments. Washington also removed an exemption that chipmakers had used for certain products designed for non-AI uses, including smartphones.

Reuters separately reported that TSMC instructed affected customers to halt orders for chips made using 16-nanometer or more advanced technology unless they obtain export licenses. The company's guidance generally limits those customers to older 28-nanometer and 40-nanometer processes, provided the designs meet conditions covering high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging. Those two technologies are important for AI processors because they help move large amounts of data quickly between chips and memory.

The timing is difficult for Chinese companies trying to diversify their suppliers. Samsung's customers include ByteDance and Kunlun, Baidu's AI chip business, according to the Financial Times. Both have sought alternative sources for AI data centers amid shortages of Nvidia processors in China. TSMC also makes smartphone chips for Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo. Those customer relationships illustrate how the rules can affect several markets at once, though the reports did not specify which individual orders had been suspended.

Investors Takeaway

The first question is how quickly the Commerce Department approves licenses for consumer chips. An industry source told the Financial Times that smartphone chip licenses were likely to be granted, but warned that the wait could still cause manufacturing delays. For TSMC and Samsung, a short pause could primarily shift when orders ship and sales are booked. A prolonged delay could leave customers scrambling to adjust production schedules.

Story Continues

The bigger question for AI is how many advanced designs Washington will allow overseas foundries to manufacture. Chinese chip designers already face capacity constraints at domestic suppliers such as Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp. If licenses are harder to obtain for AI processors, those constraints could make it more difficult to bring alternatives to Nvidia's chips to market.

news.Title: Who Is Rene Haas? What to Know About the Arm CEO as Nvidia Searches for Jensen Huang's Successor
news.Content:
Nvidia (NVDA) is looking for its next chief executive, and one potential candidate already knows the chipmaker from the inside. According to Bloomberg, the artificial intelligence (AI) darling has hired Hendrick & Struggles to help it find a successor for Jensen Huang, and the firm has recently approached Arm Holdings (ARM) top executive Rene Haas.

The Jensen Huang fiasco has taken a meaningful toll on NVDA shares, which are now down nearly 40% versus their year-to-date high.

Rene Haas Has Nvidia Experience on His Resume

Rene Haas joined Arm Holdings in 2013 to oversee its strategic alliance. But before that, he spent seven years at Nvidia, running its computing products business. The industry veteran also led Arm's intellectual property (IP) unit before ultimately taking over as its CEO in early 2022, just as Nvidia and SoftBank abandoned their proposed deal for Arm due to regulatory hurdles.

Haas then led ARM through its September 2023 debut on the Nasdaq. Earlier this year, he even pushed the company, long known for licensing its processor technology, into selling its own silicon.

Arm developed its first data center CPU with Meta Platforms (META) as its lead partner, giving it a more direct stake in what cloud giants spend on AI infrastructure.

Haas's Arm Experience Is Relevant For Nvidia

The strongest link between Haas's current job and the one Nvidia is trying to fill is already inside Nvidia's newest AI systems.

Its Vera Rubin platform pairs Rubin graphics processors with a custom Vera CPU compatible with Arm's architecture. That makes Haas's experience with processor licensing and cloud customers relevant as Nvidia sells more complete data center systems.

The stakes are already visible in NVDA results. Data centers generated $107.6 billion of its $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, and the company said its Vera Rubin NVL72 systems had already started shipping.

For investors, the succession question comes down to who can keep those systems rolling out while the biggest cloud customers develop more of their own chips.

Wall Street's Consensus View on Nvidia

Note that Wall Street remains bullish on NVDA shares under interim CEO Colette Kress. The consensus rating on Nvidia remains at Moderate Buy, with the mean price target of about $247 indicating massive upside potential from here.

news.Title: Sandisk Stock Is Worth a Third of What It Was in June. I'd Buy It Now.
news.Content:
Last week, I wrote that I'd consider starting with a small position in Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) after the stock dropped back under the price I had picked for buying it. The flash memory maker's shares have been slipping since then. They're down around 13% from their Nov. 13 close, and the company hasn't changed its guidance.

Sandisk didn't fall alone. Memory chipmaker Micron has slid around 10% in the same stretch.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Sandisk's 8-for-1 stock split takes effect after the market closes today, and split-adjusted trading is expected to start Friday morning. So I'll use split-adjusted prices throughout this piece.

On that basis, the stock trades near $96 as I write (about $770 before the split), compared to a June 25 record close of about $292. In short, shares go for about a third of their June price.

But Sandisk is earning much more now than it was then. At this price, I think the stock is a buy, and I'd be willing to hold more than a starter position.

Image source: Getty Images.

What did June's price pay for?

When the stock peaked in late June, Sandisk's latest report covered its fiscal third quarter of 2026 (its quarter ended April 3, 2026). Over the 12 months through that quarter, the company made around $4.5 billion in net income . At the June 25 close, a share cost around 81 times earnings.

Showing how fast profits have grown, Sandisk made $3.6 billion in net income in fiscal Q3 of 2026. That rose to $6.9 billion in fiscal Q4, then to $8.1 billion in fiscal Q1 of 2027 (the three months ended Oct. 2, 2026), up from just $112 million a year earlier. Revenue for fiscal Q1 rose 378% year over year to $11.0 billion. Add that up, and Sandisk's trailing 12-month net income is around $19.4 billion, more than four times the June number.

With profits up that much and the stock price down two-thirds, a buyer now pays around 6 times earnings.

Granted, the same quarterly numbers show profit growth slowing. Net income climbed 91% sequentially in fiscal Q4 yet just 17% in fiscal Q1.

Still, management's outlook for fiscal Q2 calls for revenue of $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion, which would be another quarterly gain. And it expects adjusted gross margin to stay between 84.5% and 85.5%, around the same as in fiscal Q1. Put another way, its own forecast doesn't show flash prices falling yet.

Story Continues

Buybacks and cash

The cash is coming in, too. Sandisk produced $6.3 billion in free cash flow in fiscal Q1, versus $438 million a year earlier.

It spent $5.0 billion on stock repurchases in the quarter, and across its past two fiscal quarters it bought back around 4% of its outstanding shares. Even after that spending, Sandisk closed fiscal Q1 with $5.1 billion in cash and no debt on its balance sheet.

Management said in its fiscal Q1 earnings release that it's "delivering growing and durable free cash flow." The growing part is obvious. Durable is tougher to gauge for a memory company.

Flash prices are still the risk

Almost all this hinges on what Sandisk can charge for its flash memory. And before the boom, it made very little.

In fiscal 2025 (which ended June 27, 2025), Sandisk's non-GAAP (adjusted) net income was $440 million over the whole year. Its adjusted net income in fiscal Q1 alone was $7.6 billion, more than 17 times that full-year total.

And supply might eventually catch up. In a Nov. 18 update, research firm TrendForce forecast that the flash memory market would move into oversupply in 2027. It now expects contract prices to begin dropping a quarter sooner than before, and the declines to deepen each quarter.

A slump like that could cut Sandisk's earnings a lot. But at around $96 a share, I think much of that risk is already priced in. After all, even if trailing earnings were cut in half, today's price would be about 12 times earnings.

Is Sandisk stock a buy at a third of its June price? I think it is. I'd just spread out the purchase rather than buy in one go.

I'd buy some shares now and leave the rest for after Sandisk's fiscal second-quarter results, adding then if management's outlook for the next quarter still calls for more revenue.

news.Title: Top 5 Stocks to Buy According to Billionaire Ken Fisher
news.Content:
Ken Fisher has spent more than four decades betting that big, globally dominant companies keep winning, and his latest filing shows he still believes it. Fisher Asset Management, the firm behind Fisher Investments, reported a 13F portfolio worth about $348.3 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up from roughly $335.8 billion three months earlier.

Fisher founded his firm in 1979, wrote a Forbes column for more than 32 years, and has authored 11 books. Today he serves as executive chairman and co-chief investment officer. His market call heading into the midterms was unambiguous. In an October interview, he said midterm years kick off what he considers the most consistently positive nine-month stretch in U.S. stock market history, because political gridlock blocks controversial legislation. In his words,

The stock markets celebrate when major bills fall through.

The filing backs that optimism. Across the firm's 10 largest stock positions, Fisher added shares to every one in the third quarter, from a 0.3% top-up in an industrial bellwether to a 7% increase in a weight-loss drug leader. Seven of those 10 are tech, cloud or chip companies, led by the AI chip giant now dealing with the sudden exit of its founder-CEO. The notable cut came in bonds: Fisher trimmed his 7-10 year Treasury bond fund by about 22%, to roughly 126 million shares, a move consistent with a manager leaning into stocks rather than hiding in bonds. Together, the top 10 stocks make up about a third of the portfolio.

That concentration is a bet that AI spending, cloud growth and chip demand still have years to run. It also means the portfolio will feel any AI slowdown more than most. For more on where the billionaire has been putting money to work, see the AI stocks Fisher and another billionaire were buying , and the one AI stock both piled into .

So, which stocks does Ken Fisher own the most of right now? We provided the expanded list of Top 10 Stocks to Buy According to Billionaire Ken Fisher here. The top 5 stocks are provided below.

Ken Fisher of Fisher Asset Management

Our Methodology

For this list, we scanned Fisher Asset Management, LLC's 13F portfolio for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, filed on November 6, and picked the 10 stocks with the largest percentage of the portfolio. We excluded call and put options, as well as ETFs such as bond funds. The stocks are ranked by the value of the fund's stake.

Why are we interested in the stocks that hedge funds pile into? The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points ( see more details here ).

Story Continues

5. Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN )

% of Portfolio: 2.54%

Fund's Stake Value: $8.86 billion

Amazon is Fisher's way to own both the consumer and the AI cloud in one stock. While retail drives the scale, AWS drives much of the profit, and that is where the growth now sits.

The October 29 report showed AWS re-accelerating. Cloud revenue grew 39% to $46 billion, the unit produced $17.8 billion of operating income, and its backlog reached $578 billion. Revenue commitments for Amazon's in-house Trainium chips rose more than 20x year over year, giving AWS a cheaper alternative to buying every accelerator from outside suppliers.

The price of that growth is cash. Amazon expects about $220 billion of capital spending in 2026, and trailing free cash flow has swung to roughly negative $42 billion. If AI demand cools, that build-out becomes a high fixed cost.

Fisher added about 1.7% to the position in the third quarter, betting that the spending will pay off the way Amazon's past investments did. Whether it clears this test is the key debate, which we covered here .

4. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT )

% of Portfolio: 4.00%

Fund's Stake Value: $13.92 billion

Microsoft is Fisher's AI holding with the clearest line of sight to revenue. Azure rents AI capacity to businesses, and much of that demand is already under contract.

Its fiscal first-quarter report on October 28 made that visible. Revenue of $92.3 billion beat estimates, Azure grew 48%, and commercial remaining performance obligations jumped 73% to $677 billion. That backlog gives Microsoft years of contracted cloud demand to fill, regardless of how sentiment around individual chip suppliers shifts.

The concern is spending. Capital expenditures more than doubled to about $39.4 billion in the quarter, and investors want proof that each new data center earns its keep. The stock has also lagged the broader market over the past year, which shows how much skepticism the build-out has drawn.

Fisher added about 2% to his stake in the third quarter, keeping Microsoft just behind Alphabet in the portfolio. Its spending discipline has also won over Jim Cramer, making it one of their shared AI picks .

3. Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL )

% of Portfolio: 4.02%

Fund's Stake Value: $13.99 billion

Alphabet gives Fisher a search business that funds one of the most complete AI operations in the world. It designs its own TPU chips, rents them through Google Cloud, and runs its Gemini models on top.

The October 28 report showed the cloud side taking off. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled, up 103% to $30.7 billion, and total revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion. CEO Sundar Pichai said demand for its TPU systems is strong across a wide range of customers, which signals that outside companies are buying Alphabet's chips.

The trade-off is heavy spending. Capex hit $51.4 billion in the quarter, full-year guidance rose to $195 billion to $205 billion, and Alphabet has signaled 2027 spending above $300 billion. Net income also fell year over year, to $26.2 billion.

Fisher added about 1.7% to his Class A shares in the quarter, and the stake edged past Microsoft by value. Whether the market is still undervaluing AI growth is a live debate, as our comparison with another tech giant shows .

2. Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )

% of Portfolio: 5.59%

Fund's Stake Value: $19.46 billion

Apple is Fisher's longtime core holding, and its first quarter under a new CEO gave him little reason to sell. John Ternus has taken over from Tim Cook, and his opening report was a record.

Apple's fiscal fourth quarter, reported November 2, set September-quarter records for revenue, iPhone sales and EPS. Revenue rose 12% to $114.5 billion, diluted EPS rose 14% to $2.10, and Services revenue hit an all-time high. For the full fiscal year, Apple posted record revenue of $479 billion and returned $28 billion to shareholders in the quarter alone.

The questions are margins and AI. The 47.9% gross margin included about one percentage point from tariff refunds, a boost that may not repeat. Apple is also still proving that its new Siri can compete with rivals' AI assistants, and a leadership change adds uncertainty to that push.

Fisher added about 1.5% to his stake in the quarter, keeping Apple close behind his top holding. He isn't the only well-known investor still backing it, as we explain here .

1. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA )

% of Portfolio: 6.09%

Fund's Stake Value: $21.20 billion

NVIDIA is Fisher's largest holding, and he was still buying before the turmoil began. The fund added about 1.9 million shares in the third quarter, a roughly 2% increase, bringing its stake to 92.8 million shares. Its first report since Jensen Huang's resignation suggests the business hasn't missed a beat.

Fiscal third-quarter revenue, reported November 17, jumped 103% to $115.8 billion, about $7 billion above consensus, and data center sales rose 110% to $107.6 billion. With nearly $20 billion of shipments in its first quarter, the interim CEO Colette Kress said the new Vera Rubin platform is off to an explosive start. NVIDIA guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $130 billion and raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%.

Cracks, however, are found at the edges. Gross margin is guided down to 71% to 72% from 74.9%, the outlook assumes no data center revenue from China, and the board's CEO search has no timeline. The stock still closed 2.9% lower on November 18.

Fisher's buying came before the crisis, so his next filing will show whether he still sees a bargain, as another billionaire did ahead of earnings .

news.Title: 2 Electronics Stocks to Bet On From a Prospering Industry
news.Content:
The Zacks Electronics – Miscellaneous Products industry players like KLA KLAC and SiTime SITM are benefiting from higher spending on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, data centers and cloud computing. Rising spending by hyperscalers on AI compute is increasing demand for more advanced semiconductors, networking equipment, testing, process-control and precision electronic components. Advanced chip architectures, High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) adoption, EUV, hybrid bonding and increasingly complex packaging are increasing process-control intensity and creating demand for technologies that improve yield, reliability and system performance. However, this industry is subject to fluctuations in semiconductor capital-spending cycles, macroeconomic conditions, inventory adjustments and changes in end-market demand. Supply-chain constraints, rising input costs and geopolitical trade restrictions are notable headwinds for industry participants.

Industry Description

The Zacks Electronics – Miscellaneous Products industry includes a number of original equipment manufacturers of power products, drivetrains, green energy solutions, remote-control systems, GPS navigation, home automation systems, healthcare devices, industry/factory automation, robotics, semiconductor and optical applications and energy management solutions. The industry is evolving through digital transformation and the growing demand for silicon across multiple markets. The increasing cost of manufacturing bodes well for equipment suppliers, while the growing demand for silicon is positive for semiconductor companies. Apart from the United States, companies in this industry are based in Japan, Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland. These companies either have manufacturing operations in China and Southeast Asia or generate significant revenues from these regions.

3 Trends Shaping the Future of the Industry

Solid Capital Spending Drives Prospects : Ongoing technology transition due to rapid deployment of AI is driving product complexities, which is raising the demand for solutions provided by industry participants. More complex designs, accelerating product cycles and high-value wafer volumes are growing the demand for advanced packaging. Increasing investment in expanding manufacturing capacity by semiconductor companies is a key catalyst in the long run. Since semiconductor companies are major customers of miscellaneous electronics product manufacturers, the trend bodes well for industry participants. In addition, rising spending on advanced nodes — 7 nm, 5 nm, 3 nm and 2 nm processes from logic and foundry customers — favors industry participants. Logic and foundry spending is anticipated to be healthy this year.

Story Continues

Strong Demand for AI, Data Center and Cloud Computing Solutions : Industry participants are riding on strong AI infrastructure investments, increasing compute intensity, and the need for more advanced power, thermal, automation and testing solutions. Strong hyperscaler spending, rapid advanced packaging adoption and large-scale data center buildouts are key catalysts. The rapid growth of AI workloads is increasing process complexity, driving higher demand for process control, metrology, inspection, specialty materials, precision timing and semiconductor test equipment. Meaningful recovery in industrial automation and digital infrastructure markets bodes well for industry participants.

Demand for Integrated Solutions is Rising : The industry is increasingly moving toward integrated solutions that combine compute, power, cooling, automation and energy management. This shift from discrete subsystem deployments is creating opportunities for suppliers with broad technology portfolios and systems-level capabilities.

Challenging Macroeconomic Conditions Acts as Headwind : Industry participants are suffering from challenging macroeconomic conditions globally, with enterprises in automotive, industrial and energy end-markets showing reluctance in committing to multi-year deals. Supply chains remain under pressure as companies work to secure capacity and critical components to support rapidly rising AI-driven demand, while extended lead times and infrastructure bottlenecks, particularly around power availability, are constraining the pace of data center deployment. Additionally, memory price volatility, tariff-related cost increases and the growing concentration of demand among a small number of hyperscale and AI customers are major concerns for industry players.

The group's Zacks Industry Rank, which is the average of the Zacks Rank of all member stocks, indicates bullish near-term prospects. Our research shows that the top 50% of the Zacks-ranked industries outperform the bottom 50% by a factor of more than two to one.

The Zacks Electronics – Miscellaneous Products industry has outperformed the S&P 500 and the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector in the past year.

The July 2026 acquisition of Renesas' TPD business significantly expanded SiTime's product portfolio, customer relationships and addressable market opportunities. news.Title: Cerebras Drops 20% in a Month: Is the Stock a Buy on the Dip?
news.Content:
Cerebras Systems CBRS shares have dropped 20.4% in the past month, reflecting investor concerns over its OpenAI partnership, delays in AI data center capacity deployment, margin pressure and elevated infrastructure investments. The company continues to face stiff competition from NVIDIA NVDA, Advanced Micro Devices AMD and Intel INTC in the AI space. However, strong demand for high-speed AI inference, expanding hyperscaler relationships and improving financial guidance suggest that the recent weakness could present a long-term buying opportunity. So, what should investors do with the stock? Let's dig deep to find out.

CBRS' Prospects Suffer From Data Center Delays

Concerns surrounding Cerebras' relationship with OpenAI have been a major overhang on its shares. During the third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Cerebras acknowledged that insufficient data center capacity prevented a broader rollout of OpenAI's Ultrafast offerings. CBRS management, however, rejected speculation that technical limitations were responsible and reiterated that OpenAI remains an important customer. The company disclosed delays in delivering portions of the contracted 750 megawatts of inference capacity, primarily due to land, power and building infrastructure constraints. Cerebras expects to return to its planned delivery schedule by the second half of 2027.

Profitability remains another concern for Cerebras. Despite reporting record third-quarter 2026 revenues, GAAP gross margin contracted to 20% from 40.6% in the year-ago quarter, reflecting a weaker hardware margin profile and accounting adjustments. Core hardware gross margin was 31%, pressured by shipments under older, lower-priced contracts. Meanwhile, the company reported a GAAP net loss of $161.2 million compared with $22.2 million in the prior-year quarter.

Cerebras' prospects are suffering from stiff competition from the likes of NVIDIA (NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Intel (INTC) in the AI space. NVIDIA is dominating the AI GPU market through its Blackwell, Hopper and DGX/NVL systems that are used for AI training and inference. AMD's MI300 and MI350 accelerator families are competing with CBRS in hyperscale AI infrastructure and enterprise AI clusters. Meanwhile, Intel's Gaudi AI accelerators target enterprise AI training and inference as a lower-cost GPU alternative. Shares of AMD, NVIDIA and Intel have dropped 0.8%, 30.2% and 40.4%, respectively, over the past month.

CBRS Stock's Price Performance

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Story Continues

Cerebras shares are also trading at a premium, as suggested by the Value Score of D.

Moreover, Wall Street's consensus price target implies roughly 143.04% average upside from current levels.

Robust AI Inference Demand Aids CBRS' Prospects

Cerebras continues to benefit from accelerating demand for high-speed AI inference solutions. In the third quarter of 2026, core revenues surged 70% year over year to $230.9 million, exceeding the company's guidance midpoint by approximately 7%. Core cloud and other services revenues jumped 272% to $144.9 million, highlighting growing adoption of its inference platform. CBRS raised its fourth-quarter core revenue guidance to the $310-$330 million range and 2026 forecast to the $940-$960 million range. Cerebras also expects revenues to triple in 2027, supported by expanding cloud capacity, hardware shipments and stronger customer demand.

Cerebras' expanding relationships with major cloud providers strengthen its long-term growth prospects and could reduce dependence on individual customers. The company secured partnerships with Amazon Web Services, Oracle and Microsoft, representing three hyperscaler wins over six months. Oracle plans to integrate Cerebras' high-speed inference technology into Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, with service availability expected in summer 2027. Microsoft has also signed a cloud agreement, with additional details expected in 2027. Cerebras indicated that its opportunity pipeline increased by more than tenfold during the third quarter.

Cerebras' expanding product portfolio and differentiated wafer-scale computing architecture remain important competitive advantages. The company's CS-4 AI accelerator is approaching full production and is expected to double the performance and throughput of CS-3. The next-generation CS-5 system, powered by Wafer Scale Engine 5, is targeted for production in early summer 2027 and is designed to deliver more than twice the speed of CS-4. Cerebras has also introduced production-scale heterogeneous disaggregated inference using AMD GPUs alongside its proprietary systems. CBRS estimates that this architecture can increase token generation by up to fivefold per megawatt, potentially improving inference economics and data center profitability. Unlike competing GPU architectures, Cerebras' systems do not require high-bandwidth memory, reducing exposure to memory shortages and associated cost inflation.

CBRS' Estimate Revisions Show Improving Trend

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for CBRS' 2026 earnings is pegged at 12 cents per share, against a loss of 36 cents per share over the past 30 days.

The consensus mark for fourth-quarter 2026 loss is pegged at 1 cent per share compared with a loss of 20 cents per share over the past 30 days.

Consensus Estimate Trend

Conclusion: Here's Why You Should Buy CBRS Stock

Cerebras' recent share-price weakness reflects legitimate concerns over OpenAI capacity delivery delays, customer concentration, substantial infrastructure spending and persistent GAAP losses. These factors could sustain near-term volatility. Nevertheless, accelerating AI inference demand, growing hyperscaler adoption, expanding infrastructure capacity and an improving core profitability outlook provide a compelling long-term growth narrative. The company's differentiated technology and expectations of tripling revenues in 2027 strengthen the investment case. For investors comfortable with elevated execution and valuation risks, the recent pullback could represent an attractive opportunity to gain exposure to the expanding AI inference market.

Cerebras currently has a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.

news.Title: Spotify's 9.3% ARPU Rise Signals Stronger Premium Monetization
news.Content:
Spotify Technology SPOT is seeing gains from efforts to extract more value from paying listeners. In the third quarter of 2026, premium revenues rose 17% year over year to €4.49 billion, even as premium subscriber growth was more modest at 9%. The divergence suggests that improved monetization, rather than user growth alone, is significantly contributing to the company's top line.

Premium average revenue per user (ARPU) advanced 9.3% to €4.95, or 7.5% on a constant-currency basis. Higher subscription rates helped support the increase, while differences across plans and markets partly diluted the benefit. With more revenue per account, Spotify has additional room to invest in product features, recommendation tools and subscriber retention.

Still, sustaining those benefits will require compelling product improvements that make subscribers remain engaged despite increasingly expensive plans.

Spotify Technology Revenue (TTM)

Spotify Technology revenue-ttm | Spotify Technology Quote

Advertising Adds Support to Revenue Trends

Although premium pricing provides the central investment narrative, Spotify's advertising business offers a complementary revenue stream. Ad-funded sales climbed 10% year over year, or 9% excluding currency fluctuations. Demand from automated buying platforms helped offset weaker advertising pricing, while podcast sponsorships supported further growth.

Better subscription economics and broader advertising distribution could enhance revenue resilience. However, repeated price increases may raise churn risk, particularly in price-sensitive markets, and advertisers remain exposed to shifting marketing budgets.

What Investors Should Watch

Spotify's ability to maintain subscriber additions while sustaining higher ARPU will determine whether the current monetization gains translate into durable growth. Investors should also track whether advertising improvements extend beyond volume growth into pricing stability.

How Does SPOT Compare With AAPL and AMZN?

Apple AAPL and Amazon AMZN challenge Spotify in music streaming, but their strategies differ markedly. Apple can attract listeners through integration with its devices, software and services, supporting convenience and retention across its ecosystem. Amazon benefits from a customer network and membership offerings that can encourage adoption of its music services.

Unlike Apple and Amazon, Spotify depends more directly on music and podcast engagement to generate revenues, making paid subscriber retention important. That concentration may encourage faster innovation but leaves Spotify more exposed to changes in listening preferences and subscription demand. Competition remains intense as platforms refine pricing and features.
