Foolish Take

The first thing to check for when examining a company's revenue trend is seasonality: some times of the year have stronger buying patterns than others. There usually is some seasonality for every business. To adjust for seasonality, investors often should compare one quarter to its comparable prior-year quarter to see if sales are rising or falling in that period, since reading a chart left to right could make business seem more volatile than it really is.

Qualcomm sees seasonality in its revenue, with sales peaking in December, which falls within its fiscal first quarter, but it is shown in the calendar fourth quarter in the chart. That comes from traditional holiday demand for its core smartphone customers.

TMSC also traditionally has had seasonality in its business, linked to seasonal demand for electronics. But in the chart, there is no evidence of that seasonality, as booming AI demand erases any perceived impact of consumer buying cycles.

Revenue trends like this are the most obvious metric for investors to examine when considering a stock. For Qualcomm, we see a trend of weaker sales sequentially and year-over-year. This reflects weakness in the company's mobile phone business, mainly due to steep consumer spending cuts in China.

TSMC's chart, however, is one that an investor would ideally want to see: strong sequential sales growth, indicating that demand is rising thanks to AI and data center trends.

Data source: Financial Modeling Prep. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's figures are converted from New Taiwan dollars to U.S. dollars. Data as of Nov. 17, 2026.

news.Title: Prediction: SpaceX Will Be the Largest Company in the World by 2040
news.Content:
Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) is already the sixth-most valuable company in the world, with a market capitalization approaching $2 trillion. Not too shabby, considering the company just went public in June at a valuation of about $1.8 trillion.

But I think we're only seeing the beginning of what this company could become.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Here's my prediction: By 2040, SpaceX will be the largest company in the world, surpassing Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG)(NASDAQ:GOOGL), and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN). And my prediction hinges on three things.

1. SpaceX and Tesla will merge

SpaceX had barely finished its IPO when longtime Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) bull Dan Ives put the chances of SpaceX and Tesla merging within a year at 80%. And why not? Elon Musk is the CEO of both companies, and both are focused on developing artificial intelligence and bringing new products to market. They even collaborate to some extent.

In October, Musk himself lent those rumors even more credibility when he announced that both companies had formed merger-exploration committees . Because of the inherent conflict of interest created by his massive equity stakes in the two companies, Musk isn't a member of those committees — but the effort wouldn't be happening without his blessing.

I previously projected that a combined SpaceX-Tesla company would be worth more than $5 trillion by 2029 . SpaceX has AI computing infrastructure, satellite communications, and rocket technology. Tesla adds electric vehicles, autonomous driving systems, robotics, and manufacturing capabilities.

Image source: Getty Images.

The combined company would be much more efficient, as it could develop advanced AI models, train them on its own computing infrastructure, and deploy that intelligence across Tesla's vehicles and robots.

The merger isn't guaranteed, and Tesla shareholders would need to be satisfied with the terms. But I believe it will happen.

2. SpaceX will develop the enterprise AI market

SpaceX's rocket launch business and Starlink satellite broadband service are impressive. But I don't think there's any question that AI is the company's biggest growth opportunity. In its IPO prospectus, SpaceX identified a total addressable market of $28.5 trillion for itself, which it said was the largest in human history. And of that, $22.7 trillion involves enterprise AI applications.

Story Continues

While the figure represents the potential market, and not revenue SpaceX is guaranteed to capture, even a relatively small share could become an enormous business. And SpaceX is already making plenty of headway. Its revenue in the third quarter was $14.6 billion, with the AI division generating $7.6 billion of that sum. That segment brought in just $813 million in the same quarter a year ago.

The division also recorded $431 million in operating income, reversing a $1.7 billion operating loss from the prior-year period.

SpaceX ended September with 1.7 gigawatts of installed computing capacity, and Musk has indicated that demand for the company's AI infrastructure substantially exceeds its available supply. But while renting computing power to other companies is a nice business, the real opportunity lies in SpaceX developing AI models and applications that could eventually compete for enterprise customers.

If Musk and Co. can turn even a fraction of that $22.7 trillion opportunity into recurring revenue, a $10 trillion valuation starts looking considerably more realistic.

3. Tesla will monetize its Optimus robots

Tesla is the most valuable automaker in the world and gets most of its revenue from its electric vehicles, but it is a company in transition. This year, it stopped production of its Model X and Model S vehicles to free up manufacturing capacity for the Optimus robot, and it's also halting Cybertruck production with the plan of converting those lines to make its autonomous Cybercabs.

The Optimus robot has the potential to be a big winner for Tesla. Musk describes it as a humanoid robot capable of performing tasks in factories, warehouses, and homes. Musk believes robotics could become Tesla's most important business, surpassing electric vehicles.

It plans to manufacture second-generation Optimus robots at its Texas Gigafactory, with a stated annual production capacity of 10 million units.

I don't know if we'll ever see those kinds of numbers for Optimus. But I do think the robotics business can be a growth driver if Tesla proves its robots can reliably perform useful tasks at a price customers will accept.

But imagine the opportunity if Optimus succeeds. A combined SpaceX-Tesla could develop the AI systems that power these robots, manufacture them at enormous scale, and potentially sell both the hardware and supporting software.

SpaceX's path to becoming the biggest company in the world

SpaceX isn't going to become the world's most valuable company simply by launching more rockets or adding more Starlink subscribers. But if it joins forces with Tesla, seizes a portion of the huge enterprise AI market, and turns a profit with Optimus, it's hard to see any other company matching up.

If Musk can pull this off, then his next 14 years could make his first two decades at Tesla and SpaceX look like the opening act.

news.Title: Nvidia Could Poach Arm's CEO to Replace Jensen Huang. Here's What That Might Mean for ARM Stock.
news.Content:
Nvidia's (NVDA) executive search firm has reportedly reached out to Arm Holdings (ARM) CEO Rene Haas, which makes Arm's own chief executive a leading candidate for the most scrutinized job in technology.

ARM is down just over 1% today, with the fairly muted reaction suggesting investors view the approach as far from a done deal, even though Haas's strategy has long been central to how the market values Arm.

More News from Barchart

Dear SpaceX Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 19

Dear Nvidia Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for December 10

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 20

Stop Missing Market Moves: Get the FREE Barchart Brief – your midday dose of stock movers, trending sectors, and actionable trade ideas, delivered right to your inbox. Sign Up Now!

The bigger question is whether losing Haas would actually hurt Arm, or whether the arrangement could quietly work in its favor if he lands at Nvidia.

Nvidia Slams the Door on a Huang Return

Nvidia's board has firmly ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang after his Nov. 12 resignation, with interim CEO Colette Kress holding the company steady while internal and external candidates are evaluated.

However, the backdrop is hardly calm, as Nvidia stock remains roughly 36% off its October high despite a strong quarter. It's an environment that leaves very little room for further leadership missteps.

Why Haas Fits the Nvidia Profile

Haas spent seven years at Nvidia running its computing products business before taking the helm at Arm in 2022, and the two companies share history through their failed 2020 merger attempt.

That mix of Nvidia insider knowledge and outside chief-executive experience makes him an unusually natural fit for the role, at least on paper.

That said, Nvidia's own workforce appears to favor internal continuity, with Vice President Ian Buck drawing far more support than Haas in internal sentiment surveys.

Separately, Amazon (AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos has also suggested that Nvidia should promote from within to fill the role.

What's at Stake for ARM Stock

Arm's valuation has long depended on Haas's strategy of moving the company beyond royalty licensing into data-center designs and higher-value products, a pivot that sits at the heart of the bull case.

His departure would raise questions about whether that strategy continues, and it could trigger a de-rating while Arm runs its own succession search.

On balance, the near-term risk for Arm skews modestly negative, though it stays contained until there is a formal offer or acceptance.

Story Continues

Could Arm Win by Losing Its CEO?

There is a counterargument worth weighing, since a Haas-led Nvidia could deepen its reliance on Arm-based architectures such as the Grace and Vera CPU lines.

That shift could indirectly support Arm's data-center royalty growth, an unusual scenario in which losing a chief executive to the industry's most closely watched chipmaker becomes a strategic tailwind.

Still, that benefit would be indirect, whereas the strategic uncertainty from a departure would land squarely and immediately on Arm's own shares.

Key Catalysts to Watch Next

Congressional hearings in early December could complicate Nvidia's leadership timeline, adding another layer of uncertainty to a CEO search that already has several credible contenders.

Arm investors should watch for any Nvidia board announcement, since a formal naming of Haas, or of a rival candidate such as Buck, would quickly reset expectations for ARM. Signals from Arm's own board on retention matter just as much, and either development could move the stock sharply.

For now, the market is treating the Haas headline as noise rather than news, with the price action reflecting doubt that an approach will become an offer.

Arm shareholders, in other words, are in the odd position of hoping their CEO feels flattered but not tempted.

news.Title: Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, November 19 Brings an 8-for-1 Split, But the Memory Boom May Already Be Unraveling
news.Content:
Wall Street loves a comeback story, but few have been as spectacular as Sandisk's (SNDK). Since separating from Western Digital (WDC) in February 2025, the flash-memory specialist has become one of the stock market's biggest winners, rising more than 2,000%, and riding an explosion in artificial intelligence infrastructure spending and soaring memory prices.

Yet the conditions behind that extraordinary rally may be changing. NAND flash prices have started retreating, and industry forecasts suggest more supply could be coming just as demand weakens.

More News from Barchart

Dear SpaceX Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 19

Dear Nvidia Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for December 10

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 20

Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today!

That makes tomorrow, Nov. 20, a particularly interesting date for Sandisk shareholders.

Sandisk's 8-for-1 Stock Split Arrives Tomorrow

Sandisk's much-anticipated 8-for-1 stock split takes effect after today's closing bell, with split-adjusted trading beginning Friday, Nov. 20.

For every share investors own, they'll receive seven additional shares. Someone holding 100 shares today will own 800 tomorrow. Based on Wednesday's $776.22 closing price, each share would be worth approximately $97.03 afterward. Shares are up about 7% this morning to $829.92 in early market trading.

The total investment value doesn't change. A $77,622 position remains worth $77,622, excluding subsequent market movements.

The split follows an extraordinary rally since Western Digital spun off its flash-memory business in February 2025.

Sandisk's operating performance helps explain that enthusiasm. According to its Oct. 29 earnings release, fiscal first-quarter 2027 revenue reached $11 billion, rising 23% sequentially. Net income totaled $8.1 billion, while gross margin reached 85%. Management also forecast second-quarter revenue between $12.2 billion and $12.6 billion.

Those numbers suggest the memory boom is still delivering extraordinary profits. But the next stage could look different.

A Warning Sign for the Memory Boom

Memory prices have historically moved in cycles. Manufacturers expand production to capitalize on strong demand, only to discover that additional supply eventually puts pressure on selling prices. Sandisk could be approaching another turning point.

TrendForce published a new forecast this morning predicting that NAND flash contract prices, which are expected to rise 8% to 13% in the fourth quarter, will decline between 0% and 5% in both the first and second quarters of 2027.

Story Continues

More troubling, NAND spot prices have already corrected more than 20%.

TrendForce expects global NAND bit supply to increase 25% to 30% next year, supported by $29.9 billion in industry capital expenditures. Meanwhile, Chinese cloud providers are reducing enterprise SSD orders enough to offset additional demand from North American customers.

That's a potentially uncomfortable combination: more memory chips competing for fewer incremental orders.

The risk is particularly relevant to Sandisk because, unlike Micron Technology (MU), which also produces DRAM and high-bandwidth memory, Sandisk concentrates on NAND flash and related storage products.

Falling NAND prices could therefore pressure Sandisk's margins even if AI infrastructure spending continues growing.

What SNDK Investors Should Watch Next

Granted, falling spot prices don't immediately translate into lower contract revenue. Sandisk's latest results demonstrate that its customers are still paying premium prices, while its 85% gross margin provides room to absorb some pricing pressure. And strong AI demand could keep the industry tighter than TrendForce anticipates.

Still, investors should remember that Sandisk's remarkable rally has depended heavily on favorable NAND pricing. If prices reverse while manufacturers continue expanding production, the earnings outlook could change quickly.

That makes the next several quarters more consequential than tomorrow's split. Investors should watch whether Sandisk maintains its revenue guidance, whether gross margins begin narrowing, and whether TrendForce's anticipated oversupply actually develops.

The Bottom Line

Sandisk's 8-for-1 split makes its shares more accessible, but it doesn't make the underlying business more valuable. The company is generating record profits, yet the first signs of another NAND pricing downturn are appearing just as manufacturers prepare to increase supply.

For shareholders, Nov. 20 marks an exciting milestone. But the more important date may be early 2027, when Sandisk's extraordinary memory boom faces its first real test.

news.Title: Why Sandisk Stock Finally Popped Today
news.Content:
I may have been early, but at least I was right.

For days, I've been arguing that the steep sell-off in Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) stock was creating a buying opportunity for investors. For just as many days (five straight), Sandisk stock has defied my predictions and gone nowhere but down.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Until today. Today , Sandisk stock did a U-Turn and ran up 7.5% through 10:05 a.m.

And you probably have Lynx Equity to thank for it.

Image source: Getty Images.

Lynx loves Micron (and likes Sandisk, too)

In a note out on StreetInsider.com this morning, Rajkumar argues that even if data center construction slows in the U.S. (and it might), this doesn't necessarily mean demand for memory chips will weaken. AI data centers aren't the only users of memory chips, for one thing. For another, tighter regulations and higher costs to build data centers might soon be offset by a wave of money going to one of the bigger AI users, Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT), which begins trading as a public stock today.

Rajkumar said all this in support of Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stock, a maker of NAND and DRAM memory chips that Lynx supports. In this analyst's opinion, a 17% drop in Micron's share price over the past month leaves Micron stock "ridiculously cheap," trading at only $750 per share and likely to rise to $1,325 per share over the next 12 months.

But I wonder: If Micron stock is "ridiculously cheap"... what does that make Sandisk?

What's next for Sandisk

Priced at just 6.4 times trailing earnings today, Sandisk costs 33% less than Micron stock on a trailing price-to-earnings basis. On forward P/E, the discount gets cut in half, but that still leaves Sandisk looking 17% cheaper than Micron.

Granted, analysts polled by S&P Global Market Intelligence see Micron outgrowing Sandisk slightly over the next five years -- 43% versus 40%. But given the disparities in price, I still think Sandisk is the cheaper choice.

news.Title: Not AMD. Not Intel. This Is the Chip Stock Wall Street Is Underestimating
news.Content:
So far, there are surely many investors who want to put November behind them. Companies like Nvidia are among those having a rough month, considering the tech stock sell-off, the backlash against data centers, and a scandal that cost Jensen Huang his job as CEO .

Understandably, some shareholders are getting a little nervous. And if you're looking for another way to invest in artificial intelligence, there are certainly options. Advanced Micro Devices and Intel are two obvious candidates, but I think Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) deserves a lot more love than it's getting.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

On Nov. 13, Rothschild & Co Redburn downgraded Broadcom stock from "Buy" to "Neutral" and cut its price target from $595 to $398. That's nearly $200 wiped off the analyst's expectations in one shot.

But hold the phone: Broadcom's revenue is growing at a rapid pace. Its AI business is exploding, and it's generating billions in cash. Even so, the stock price is essentially in 2026. Let's see what's going on.

Image source: Getty Images.

Take a look at these numbers

Broadcom's revenue for its fiscal third quarter (ended Aug. 2) was $29.6 billion, up 86% from a year ago. And its AI semiconductor business did even better, generating $16.7 billion in revenue, an incredible 221% increase.

The chipmaker doesn't expect things to slow down, either. Management issued guidance for $21.7 billion in AI semiconductor revenue in the fourth quarter, up another 236% from a year ago.

Broadcom competes with Nvidia in the AI accelerator space, but it takes a different tack. While Nvidia's all-powerful graphics processing units can do pretty much anything that a company needs to train and run AI programs, Broadcom's custom AI accelerators are chips designed around the specific needs of large technology customers.

If companies want to build their own AI chips rather than relying entirely on Nvidia, Broadcom is one company they can turn to for that purpose.

Broadcom generated $13.7 billion in free cash flow in the third quarter, compared with $7 billion a year earlier. That means the company nearly doubled its cash generation while growing revenue by 86%. What's not to like?

But what about that downgrade?

Rothschild & Co Redburn points out that Broadcom is counting heavily on companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to keep spending enormous sums on AI infrastructure. And neither AI start-up has demonstrated that it can sustain that spending from its own cash generation.

Story Continues

Anthropic recently announced a $63 billion financing arrangement to fund computing infrastructure powered by Broadcom's custom AI chips and networking technology. Broadcom also has financial exposure to Anthropic's ability to meet some of its obligations.

That's a pretty substantial bet on a company that's still losing money. But investors should also recognize that Broadcom has more going for it than AI chips.

Its infrastructure software business, which includes VMware, generated $8.75 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 29% year over year. That's nearly 30% of Broadcom's total business, and it gives the company another way to make money from businesses investing in their computing infrastructure.

Broadcom is also bringing AI capabilities to VMware, including tools that allow companies to run AI applications in private cloud environments. So while the biggest AI developers get the headlines, Broadcom is selling technology to a much wider group of customers.

Is Broadcom stock worth buying?

I wouldn't ignore the risks involving Anthropic and OpenAI. If their spending plans unravel, Broadcom could have a serious problem. And the stock isn't immune to the broader pullback in AI investments.

But Broadcom's business is delivering results right now. Revenue is soaring, free cash flow is growing, and its custom chips have become an important alternative to Nvidia's processors.

Investors will get another update when Broadcom reports earnings on Dec. 9. With the stock essentially flat this year, I think there's a compelling argument that Wall Street is paying too much attention to what could go wrong and not enough to what's already going right.

news.Title: Amkor's Computing Business Gains Momentum: Is More Growth Ahead?
news.Content:
Amkor Technology AMKR is positioned for sustained Computing revenue growth through 2027 as artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure demand accelerates and advanced packaging programs scale. In third-quarter 2026, Computing revenues surged 37% year over year and 25% sequentially to a record, lifting the segment's share of total sales to 26% from 19% a year earlier. This growing contribution highlights Computing's increasing importance to Amkor's revenue mix.

The momentum reflects the ongoing ramp of Amkor's flagship high-density fan-out (HDFO) CPU program and the start of an additional HDFO CPU program for a hyperscaler in third-quarter 2026. Two 2.5D programs for networking and data centers were expected to begin ramping in the fourth quarter, broadening its exposure beyond traditional CPUs. The company expects Computing revenues to grow at a low-double-digit rate sequentially in the fourth quarter, translating to more than 50% year-over-year growth.

Looking further ahead, management projected more than 30% Computing growth in 2026 and a similar or higher rate in 2027. Expansion in Korea, including two new buildings at Gwangju and additional test capacity at Songdo, should support data center demand. Long-term capacity commitments and advance customer payments also provide greater visibility into future production needs.

However, weaker PC demand and elevated memory costs could limit growth; meanwhile, the complex, more-than-300-step HDFO production process creates ramp-up execution risks. Heavy investments in new capacity may also increase depreciation and pressure margins if utilization falls short of expectations. Yet, robust AI-related demand, new program ramps and growing capacity support a favorable Computing revenue outlook through 2027.

How Do the Competitors Compare to AMKR?

Intel INTC competes with Amkor through its advanced semiconductor packaging capabilities targeting AI and high-performance computing. Intel's Foveros 3D stacking and Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB) technologies enable complex chiplet integration, competing with Amkor's HDFO and 2.5D solutions. Intel is expanding its advanced packaging capabilities in New Mexico to attract external foundry customers, strengthening its position in AI infrastructure.

GlobalFoundries GFS competes with Amkor through advanced packaging, heterogeneous integration and 2.5D/3D technologies. GlobalFoundries is expanding its U.S. packaging ecosystem through a $2 billion multiyear agreement with TSMC to manufacture silicon interposers for AI and high-performance computing applications. GlobalFoundries' expanding packaging capabilities and integrated manufacturing services strengthen its ability to capture demand for complex semiconductor architectures, intensifying competition with Amkor.

news.Title: 174-year-old American bank’s Bitcoin exposure nears Tesla and SpaceX
news.Content:
When people think of big Bitcoin holders, they usually picture tech companies, not a traditional bank. Wells Fargo's latest filing suggests that picture may need updating.

Wells Fargo reported 49,577,094 shares of BlackRock 's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, according to its quarterly 13F filing .

The stake was worth about $2.35 billion, spread across five lines from different parts of the bank.

IBIT is an exchange-traded fund that holds Bitcoin directly and trades like a stock. Each share represents a small slice of the fund's Bitcoin.

Related: Analyst warns Anthropic IPO is pulling money out of Bitcoin

About 28,000 Bitcoin, indirectly

IBIT held 801,033 Bitcoin against 1,414,760,000 shares outstanding on Sept. 30, according to its quarterly report .

At that ratio, Wells Fargo's shares equal about 28,070 Bitcoin.

Tesla held 11,509 Bitcoin as of Sept. 30, bought for $386 million, according to its quarterly report .

SpaceX held 18,712 Bitcoin, according to its IPO filing , the same amount it reported at the end of both 2024 and 2025. Together, the two companies hold 30,221 Bitcoin.

That puts Wells Fargo's exposure at about 93% of the two companies' combined holdings. It already tops either one on its own.

A stake that grew all year

The holding grew fast.

At the end of March, Wells Fargo reported about 6.5 million IBIT shares, worth roughly $250 million, according to an amended filing for that quarter.

By the end of June, that had grown to 24,396,222 shares, worth about $812.2 million, according to its June filing .

Popular on TheStreet Roundtable:

Goldman, Citi and other big banks put $270 million behind their own stablecoin

AI-linked tokens tumble as doubts emerge over tech boom

Billionaire Paul Tudor Jones doubles stake in BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF

Its share count then about doubled again by September, and the value nearly tripled as Bitcoin rose during the quarter.

Wells Fargo also reported options on IBIT: puts covering 540,000 shares and calls covering 717,200. A put profits if a price falls, and a call profits if it rises.

Mostly clients, not the bank

The headline number comes with a big caveat. 13F filings include shares held for clients through brokerage and advisory accounts, not just the bank's own money.

The filing doesn't show how much belongs to Wells Fargo itself.

In practice, that makes this less a story about a bank buying Bitcoin and more about its customers, who are using ETFs to get Bitcoin exposure inside traditional accounts.

The figures reflect positions on Sept. 30, before Bitcoin's sharp fall. Bitcoin traded at $63,058 at 18:18 UTC on Nov. 18, according to Decibel , well below its quarter-end level.

news.Title: How to Play SNDK Stock After Sandisk’s 8-for-1 Stock Split
news.Content:
Stock splits often generate excitement on Wall Street, particularly when they involve companies that have delivered extraordinary returns to shareholders. And Sandisk (SNDK) certainly fits that description. Since its separation from Western Digital (WDC) last year, the memory chipmaker has emerged as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with surging demand for data storage fueling impressive growth in its business and stock price. Now, Sandisk is preparing for an 8-for-1 stock split, with its shares set to begin trading on a split-adjusted basis on Friday, Nov. 20.

But the timing of the split is far from ideal. After an extraordinary rally that sent SNDK shares soaring to record highs, the stock has suffered a brutal correction amid growing concerns about the sustainability of the AI spending boom. A combination of macroeconomic uncertainty, shifting political dynamics, and fresh challenges facing the semiconductor industry has made investors increasingly cautious about some of the market's biggest AI winners. And for a company whose fortunes are closely tied to demand for memory chips, these developments raise important questions about whether its impressive growth trajectory can continue.

More News from Barchart

Dear SpaceX Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 19

Dear Nvidia Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for December 10

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 20

Stop Missing Market Moves: Get the FREE Barchart Brief – your midday dose of stock movers, trending sectors, and actionable trade ideas, delivered right to your inbox. Sign Up Now!

That leaves investors facing an interesting dilemma. Could the lower share price and recent selloff create an attractive opportunity to gain exposure to one of the AI boom's standout performers, or are there deeper risks lurking beneath the company's impressive financial results? And, more importantly, how should existing shareholders and prospective buyers approach SNDK stock as the split takes effect? Let's take a closer look.

About Sandisk Stock

Sandisk is a leading developer and manufacturer of data storage devices and solutions based on NAND flash technology. The company was spun off from hard-drive manufacturer Western Digital last year. It offers products such as solid-state drives (SSDs), removable memory cards (SD, microSD, CompactFlash), USB flash drives, and embedded storage for mobile and automotive applications. Sandisk's storage chips, known as NAND flash memory, have become increasingly vital in AI data centers and consumer devices, fueling unprecedented growth for the company. SNDK's market cap currently stands at $113.4 billion.

Story Continues

Shares of the memory supplier have soared 244% year-to-date (YTD), driven by booming demand for data storage. However, the stock has undergone a sharp correction since October, plunging from around $1,800 to below $850. The selloff came as concerns over the sustainability of AI spending mounted, fueled by expectations that U.S. interest rates would remain higher for longer and that a continued rise in memory prices could eventually weigh on demand. Capital spending updates from hyperscalers then added to the pressure. More recently, the Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections, Jensen Huang's shock departure as Nvidia's CEO, and new U.S. restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips further dampened investor sentiment.

Sandisk's 8-for-1 Stock Split: What Investors Need to Know

On Oct. 29, Sandisk announced an 8-for-1 forward stock split alongside its fiscal Q1 2027 results. That means Sandisk shareholders will end up owning more shares, though the split changes nothing from a fundamental standpoint.

Under the arrangement, shareholders will receive seven additional shares for each share they own as of the market close on Nov. 19, with SNDK set to begin trading on a split-adjusted basis when the Nasdaq opens on Friday, Nov. 20. For example, if the stock trades at $800 before the split, its post-split price would be $100, while an investor who owned one share would hold eight shares. With that, the market value of an investor's SNDK holdings will remain unchanged after the split, with only the share price and number of shares changing.

Still, the lower share price could have some practical benefits. Sandisk itself noted that its shares had climbed significantly since its separation from Western Digital, making the split a way to improve accessibility. A lower share price could make the stock more approachable for retail investors and employees, particularly where fractional-share trading is unavailable or less convenient.

Under normal circumstances, the split would likely have provided a short-term boost to sentiment, but amid growing volatility in the AI trade, SNDK investors have much bigger questions to grapple with.

Record Gross Margins Raise Questions About the Memory Cycle

The main driver of explosive growth in Sandisk's top and bottom lines is booming demand for high-capacity storage as AI infrastructure expands. AI applications require massive amounts of NAND flash storage to store datasets, model files, checkpoints, and information retrieved by AI systems. These rapidly improving fundamentals have been more than reflected in SNDK's stock price, which has posted triple-digit gains so far this year.

However, the company's surging profitability may have a downside, particularly given the boom-and-bust cycles that have historically defined the memory industry. As gross margins, among the most closely watched metrics for memory chipmakers, approach extreme levels, investors begin to question whether they are sustainable. That, in turn, raises the question of whether the cycle has reached its peak.

Sandisk reported a record non-GAAP gross margin of 85.1% in fiscal Q1. Meanwhile, management forecast a non-GAAP gross margin of 84.5% to 85.5% in fiscal Q2, with the 85% midpoint implying a slight sequential decline. Although the projected drop was just 10 basis points, it was enough to reignite concerns that the current memory cycle may be peaking.

Another important point is that Sandisk's gross margins are driven primarily by market pricing and customer demand rather than fluctuations in manufacturing input costs. That means any slowdown in memory chip demand could put downward pressure on prices and squeeze the company's gross margins, potentially signaling the start of a downturn in the industry's cycle. This helps explain why SNDK stock has come under such intense pressure lately, weighed down by concerns about tighter AI regulation following the Democratic sweep, uncertainty over Nvidia's role as the "AI central bank" after Huang's downfall, and new U.S. restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips. All of these factors could ultimately weaken demand for memory chips.

To be sure, Sandisk executives have stressed that the NAND industry is undergoing a "structural shift," with demand patterns "changing materially" from those seen in previous cycles. That argument has some backing, as management said on its latest earnings call that long-term agreements cover roughly 50% of fiscal 2027 bit supply and about two-thirds of fiscal 2028 bit supply. However, I believe that to meaningfully ease concerns about cyclicality, we would need to see at least 70% of supply locked in under long-term agreements for each of the next three years.

How to Play SNDK Stock After the Split

For existing shareholders, the stock split makes little difference. Their ownership stakes and the economic value of their holdings will remain the same. The more important question is whether Sandisk can sustain its exceptional margins in the face of mounting challenges.

For prospective investors, the lower post-split share price may make the stock feel more accessible, but it should not be mistaken for a cheaper valuation. And that same question is just as significant for anyone considering buying SNDK stock.

Still, I have to admit that the recent pullback makes the setup more interesting. Sandisk was recently trading within the $770–$800 support zone. We've already seen the importance of this zone, as the stock initially bounced from it to the $1,000 level. So far, it appears that the stock can hold this support and is already showing early signs of bullish momentum, at least during this morning's early trading. I believe the risk-reward could be favorable for initiating a new position or adding to an existing one to lower the average cost basis. And if the stock breaks below this zone, I would turn my attention to the $680–$700 area, applying the same logic.

news.Title: Why It’s Time to Buy the Pullback in Qualcomm Stock
news.Content:
Qualcomm (QCOM) stock has been under pressure, declining more than 38% from its 52-week high. The loss of Apple (AAPL) revenue and the adverse impact of rising memory costs on its handset business have weighed on its revenue and profitability.

The impact is evident in the company's fiscal 2026 results. Qualcomm reported revenue of $43.1 billion, down 3% from $44.3 billion in fiscal 2025. The company's core Qualcomm CDMA Technologies (QCT) business also saw revenue decline 3% year-over-year (YOY), largely due to weaker handset sales. However, strength in the automotive and Internet of Things (IoT) businesses supported its top line, while revenue from its Qualcomm Technology Licensing (QTL) segment remained broadly flat.

More News from Barchart

Dear SpaceX Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 19

Dear Nvidia Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for December 10

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 20

Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today!

Profitability also took a hit. Adjusted EPS fell 12% YOY to $12.03 in fiscal 2026, reflecting weaker handset performance and continued margin pressure.

Despite these near-term challenges, there are reasons to remain optimistic about Qualcomm's prospects. Much of the negative news is already reflected in the price of QCOM stock. At the same time, its growing pipeline of opportunities across automotive, IoT, data center, and other markets provides a solid base for growth.

Qualcomm Is Set for Stronger Growth

Qualcomm entered fiscal 2027 strong, supported by its strategic shift toward revenue diversification, a solid data-center revenue opportunity, and ongoing strength in automotive.

Qualcomm expects non-handset revenues within its QCT segment — which is comprised of automotive, IoT, and data center — to increase by more than 60% YOY. These businesses are also projected to contribute more than 50% of total QCT revenues during the fiscal year, highlighting Qualcomm's gradual transition away from its traditional dependence on the smartphone market.

The data-center business is expected to become a significant growth contributor as Qualcomm moves from customer engagements to commercial shipments. Management has reaffirmed its revenue targets of $5 billion for fiscal 2027 and $15 billion for fiscal 2029, with the business expected to exit fiscal 2027 at an annualized revenue run rate (ARR) of approximately $7 billion. Initial shipments to two hyperscaler customers are expected to help generate more than $650 million in data-center revenue in the December quarter.

Story Continues

Furthermore, Qualcomm's strategic agreement with Amazon's (AMZN) Amazon Web Services presents a revenue opportunity of up to $60 billion over the next decade, while additional engagements with hyperscalers could further strengthen its long-term growth pipeline.

Qualcomm's automotive business is also demonstrating strong momentum, achieving an $8 billion ARR by the end of fiscal 2026. At the same time, investments in agentic artificial intelligence (AI), AI accelerators, and CPU platforms are positioning the company to capitalize on emerging computing requirements and create new product opportunities.

In QTL, Qualcomm has completed long-term agreements with major customers, including Apple, Huawei, and Transsion. These renewals provide greater revenue visibility and reduce near-term licensing uncertainty, while management expects the long-term QTL revenue outlook to remain unchanged. Additionally, planned product price increases to offset higher semiconductor input costs are expected to support QCT gross margins, with the full benefits likely to materialize in the second half of fiscal 2027.

Overall, Qualcomm's prospects remain solid, driven by a structural shift toward a more diversified revenue base. Expanding data-center operations, resilient automotive demand, AI-related investments, and stable licensing revenues provide multiple growth drivers.

Qualcomm's Diversified Growth Story Makes the Pullback Worth Buying

Wall Street analysts have a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating for QCOM stock. However, the pullback presents an attractive opportunity for long-term investors, as Qualcomm's growth prospects extend well beyond the challenged smartphone market. Although the loss of Apple-related revenue, weaker handset demand, and rising memory costs have weighed on its recent financial performance, the company's expanding automotive, IoT, and data-center businesses offer meaningful growth opportunities.

Moreover, renewed licensing agreements and planned product price increases should provide additional support to revenue visibility and margins. While near-term volatility may persist, Qualcomm's expanding growth pipeline and strategic positioning in AI infrastructure strengthen its investment case.

news.Title: Analysts Turned Bullish on These 5 Stocks on Tuesday
news.Content:
Wall Street is trading on what the Federal Reserve does next, even as analysts keep changing their ratings. The Fed held its key rate steady at its October 27 to 28 meeting, after raising it in September for the first time in three years.

Minutes released on November 18 showed that nearly all officials expect a quarter-point increase in December, and two raised the idea of a half-point move. Wall Street puts the odds of a December hike near 95%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

The jump in expectations began on November 10, when a hotter-than-expected October inflation report sent the 2-year Treasury yield up more than 18 basis points, its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, Reuters reported.

Why the Fed May Not Be Done Raising Rates

Fed Governor Christopher Waller backs the larger move. He said inflation is "headed in the wrong direction and it's spreading out," and he put core inflation at about a 3.5% annual rate over the past three months, against the Fed's 2% target. Readers following analysts' favorite growth names can find more in our ranking of aggressive growth picks from Wall Street analysts .

New York Fed President John Williams disagrees and does not think the situation calls for dramatic action. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has said the economy will likely need several rate increases before spring 2027, and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly leans toward more hikes because she worries that companies are passing higher costs on to consumers.

Treasury Yields Back Above 5% Draw Investor Attention

The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.36% on October 7, its highest level in regular trading since 2002, and it was on pace on November 17 for its 27th close above 5% this year, Bloomberg reported. All of 2007 had 29 such closes. Analysts are still finding value at these levels, as our list of affordable stocks to buy according to Wall Street analysts shows.

JPMorgan Asset Management portfolio manager Priya Misra said yields above 5% reflect a "risk premium due to uncertainty about the Fed." Dan Carter of Fort Washington Investment Advisors said fixed income offers better risk and reward than it has in some time, and that the stock rally since 2023 may push many portfolios to rebalance toward bonds. 4. Humana (NYSE:HUM)

Average Upside Potential: 32%

Bernstein raised its price target on Humana to $515 from $425 on November 17 and kept its Outperform rating. The firm said stable medical use and industry pricing discipline support a recovery in Medicare Advantage margins.

Humana sells Medicare Advantage and other health insurance plans and runs the CenterWell care business. In the third quarter of 2026, Humana reported GAAP earnings of $1.33 per share but an adjusted loss of $0.70 per share, against adjusted earnings of $3.24 a year earlier, as revenue grew. Humana reported those results on November 6, 2026. It raised its 2026 adjusted earnings guidance to at least $9.50.

On November 18, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposed a rule that would tighten oversight of Medicare, Medicaid and the health insurance marketplace, with more audits of insurers and a way for the agency to recover improper payments, and Humana was among the insurers whose shares fell. Public comment on the proposal is open until January 19, 2027. We wrote about how Humana expects most of its members to be in four-star plans before that.

3. M-tron Industries (NYSEAMERICAN:MPTI)

Average Upside Potential: 34%

Freedom Broker analyst Sergey Glinyanov upgraded M-tron Industries to Buy from Hold on November 17 even as he cut his price target to $84 from $88, citing "lower valuation multiples and a higher discount rate." He still raised his estimates for 2026 through 2028, with the biggest increase in 2028 on missile programs for Raytheon and Lockheed Martin.

M-tron makes frequency and spectrum control products, such as oscillators and filters, for aerospace and defense customers. Revenue in the third quarter of 2026 rose to $15.7 million, and backlog stood at $84.9 million on September 30, up from the end of 2025. M-tron reported those results on November 12, before Freedom Broker moved to Buy.

Glinyanov expects 2027 to be a transition year, with costs for added capacity and new hires weighing on results. He also sees the company's radar business growing from under $2 million to about $8 million a year. Management cautioned that backlog could dip in the fourth quarter, which Freedom Broker attributed to contract timing rather than weaker demand. Freedom Broker also called the September 30 backlog a record high.

2. Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO)

Average Upside Potential: 35%

HSBC upgraded Cisco to Buy from Hold on November 17 and raised its price target to $133 from $120, pointing to growth in AI networking.

Cisco designs and sells the networking equipment and software that connect company and cloud data centers. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue rose 24% from a year earlier, and Chief Executive Officer Chuck Robbins said, "We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle." The company expects $9 billion in AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers in fiscal 2027, more than double the total for fiscal 2026. Product revenue grew faster than total revenue in the first quarter, which ended on October 24, 2026.

Robbins, who spoke when the company reported on November 12, also said the quarter brought Cisco's strongest revenue and earnings per share growth in more than 15 years, and the company raised its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP earnings per share guidance to $5.47 to $5.53. Our analysis of whether Cisco can profit from helping customers spend less on AI takes up the other side of that demand.

1. Praxis Precision Medicines (NASDAQ:PRAX)

Average Upside Potential: 120%

Wells Fargo analyst Ben Burnett upgraded Praxis Precision Medicines to Overweight from Equal Weight on November 17 and raised his price target to $509 from $343. He said the company's investor day on November 12 had eased his concerns about the endpoint in its ulixacaltamide trial.

Praxis develops treatments for brain disorders such as essential tremor and rare genetic forms of epilepsy. The FDA's target decision date for relutrigine, which treats two types of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, is December 27, 2026, and the date for ulixacaltamide, for essential tremor, is January 29, 2027. Chief Executive Officer Marcio Souza said, "We are entering a defining period for Praxis, with two key regulatory milestones ahead."

The company ended the third quarter of 2026 with about $1.3 billion in cash and investments, which it expects to fund operations into 2028. Its net loss widened to $94.2 million from $73.9 million a year earlier, and the company also expects results from its EMERALD trial in the fourth quarter of 2026. Praxis said the relutrigine team is fully hired and that it expects the ulixacaltamide sales force to be in place in the fourth quarter of 2026.

news.Title: Why It’s Time to Buy the Pullback in Intel Stock
news.Content:
Intel (INTC) stock has witnessed a steep correction, eroding a substantial portion of its year-to-date (YTD) gains. INTC stock has fallen more than 61% from its 52-week high and about 39% over the past month.

Multiple factors have dragged Intel stock down, including disappointing fourth-quarter revenue guidance, manufacturing capacity constraints, rising memory prices, tighter corporate IT budgets, and broader weakness across artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks. These challenges are significant for Intel's Client Computing business, where demand conditions have weakened considerably.

More News from Barchart

Dear Nvidia Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for December 10

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 20

Markets move fast. Keep up by reading our FREE midday Barchart Brief newsletter for exclusive charts, analysis, and headlines.

However, the recent decline has created a more attractive risk-reward profile. Although the PC market remains under pressure, Intel's Data Center and AI (DCAI) business is witnessing strong growth, supported by increasing demand for server processors and purpose-built silicon. This segment remains a key growth driver as the company navigates near-term challenges.

Weak PC Demand and Cautious Revenue Guidance Weigh on Sentiment

A disappointing outlook for Q4 followed Intel's latest quarterly results. Management projected revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion, below analysts' expectations of more than $17 billion. The weaker guidance raised concerns about the company's near-term revenue trajectory, especially as capital expenditures and component procurement commitments are expected to increase over the coming quarters.

The pressure is most evident in the PC market. Rising memory prices and limited component availability have increased system costs, further constraining demand in an environment where corporate IT budgets remain tight. Intel also indicated that its original equipment manufacturer (OEM) partners have accelerated inventory adjustments in response to weaker end-market sales.

Management expects these conditions to persist until memory supply improves and pricing stabilizes. Its current projections suggest that the PC market could face a prolonged downturn rather than a temporary slowdown.

Intel anticipates that the total addressable market (TAM) for PC units will contract, while the second half of 2027 could show some improvement. These projections highlight the risks facing Intel's client computing business. Consequently, expectations for a meaningful near-term recovery in PC-related revenue should remain cautious.

Story Continues

The DCAI Business Provides a Strong Growth Counterbalance

While the PC business faces cyclical and supply-related headwinds, Intel's DCAI segment is delivering considerably stronger results. DCAI revenue reached $7.3 billion in Q3, increasing 17% sequentially and 78% year-over-year (YOY). Growth was broad-based, driven by hyperscale cloud providers, enterprise customers, and emerging neocloud operators.

Purpose-built silicon is emerging as another important growth driver for Intel. Revenue from this business increased more than 50% sequentially and more than doubled YOY. Management noted that the segment has tripled in size over the past three years and expects it to triple again over the coming years.

The opportunity is supported by growing demand for customized computing solutions, particularly among AI infrastructure providers and hyperscale customers. Intel is expanding its intellectual property (IP) portfolio to address a broader range of customer requirements, including opportunities with existing clients, new customers, and AI-focused companies.

The company has also introduced Crescent Island, an inference-optimized GPU designed to address the growing demand for AI inference workloads. Initial customer feedback has been encouraging, and management indicated that product performance is progressing as expected.

Another catalyst is the significant demand for CPUs as AI infrastructure evolves. The emergence of agentic AI applications increases server CPU requirements. As AI systems move beyond conventional model training toward more complex inference and autonomous workloads, demand for general-purpose computing capacity could expand. This creates an opportunity for Intel to benefit from broader data-center spending.

Intel Stock's Pullback Is an Opportunity

Wall Street maintains a consensus "Hold" rating on INTC stock as Intel navigates near-term PC market weakness. While cautious revenue guidance, manufacturing constraints, and rising component costs could continue to pressure results, the strong momentum in DCAI and purpose-built silicon provides a meaningful growth counterbalance. Increasing CPU demand from AI infrastructure and the company's expanding presence in customized silicon strengthen its longer-term prospects.

Therefore, the recent pullback presents an attractive entry point for investors considering Intel stock.

Its RX-400 and EX-400 5G RedCap routers moved into full-scale production during the second quarter, with customer wins converting into shipments. Continued adoption of these products, along with investments in AirLink's software platform and security capabilities, could have supported growth in the company's IoT systems and connectivity business.

The high-end consumer business is also expected to have contributed to the company's growth in the third quarter. Management expects revenues from this end market to increase, supported by seasonal demand, market-share gains in TVS products and contributions from the company's sensing portfolio. The company's efforts to extend its protection franchise into power-delivery applications and to broaden its sensing portfolio are also expected to have supported growth.

Semtech's optical roadmap might have benefited from the integration of HieFo, which expands its photonics capabilities for next-generation optical applications. Investment Consideration

Semtech remains well-positioned to benefit from rising investments in AI data centers and the growing demand for high-speed connectivity solutions. Its CopperEdge and FiberEdge products are gaining traction as the industry transitions from 800G to 1.6T connectivity. Strong demand from hyperscalers and optical module manufacturers, along with increasing adoption of 1.6T products, provides significant growth opportunities. The company expects its 1.6T portfolio to become a major contributor to data center revenues, supported by its strong position in linear equalizers, TIAs and driver solutions.

Semtech is also benefiting from growing adoption of its LoRa technology across industrial, commercial, smart home and security applications. Its LoRaWAN, LoRa Plus and Amazon Sidewalk offerings provide exposure to multiple growth markets. In addition, Semtech is expanding its photonics portfolio through gain chips, high-power CW lasers, semiconductor optical amplifiers and photodiodes. These offerings could help increase its content per optical transceiver from high single-digit dollars to high double-digit dollars as the industry moves toward 3.2T connectivity, creating additional long-term growth opportunities.

news.Title: The Zacks Analyst Blog Highlights NVIDIA, Cisco Systems and AMD
news.Content:
For Immediate Release

Chicago, IL – November 19, 2026 – Zacks.com announces the list of stocks featured in the Analyst Blog. Every day the Zacks Equity Research analysts discuss the latest news and events impacting stocks and the financial markets. Stocks recently featured in the blog include: NVIDIA Corporation NVDA, Cisco Systems, Inc CSCO and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD.

Here are highlights from Wednesday's Analyst Blog:

NVIDIA vs. Cisco: One AI Stock Looks Like a Better Buy Now

Despite NVIDIA Corporation 's strong quarterly performance, leadership uncertainty and rising artificial intelligence (AI) spending concerns could pose a challenge in the future. However, Cisco Systems, Inc. 's stable management and diversified business portfolio could position it as a better stock to buy now. Let's explore –

NVIDIA Sees Record Growth, Issues Strong Q4 Revenue Guidance

NVIDIA delivered another strong quarter, with revenues surging 103% year over year to $115.8 billion in the fiscal third quarter of 2027, according to the company's Nov. 17 press release. It also posted a 20% sequential rise from $96.2 billion in the previous quarter. NVIDIA's triple-digit growth rate highlighted that strong AI spending benefited the company, with tech companies investing significantly in computing capacity.

The Data Center business remains its primary growth driver, with revenues jumping 110% year over year and 21% sequentially to $107.6 billion. This result shows NVIDIA is making the most of hyperscalers' massive investments in AI-driven data centers. By the way, NVIDIA is converting its impressive revenue growth into noteworthy profits as well. Its GAAP net income jumped 105% year over year to $65.3 billion.

Looking ahead, NVIDIA expects revenues of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, in the fiscal fourth quarter of 2027, which would represent a 12% sequential rise. That's a strong revenue growth projection, especially since it doesn't include China-related Data Center compute revenues. NVIDIA also expects its earnings outlook to remain strong in the fiscal fourth quarter.

NVIDIA Is Dominating AI, But Is Cisco the Better Investment?

NVIDIA's strong fiscal third-quarter performance and optimistic fiscal fourth-quarter outlook suggest the company is not only benefiting from the AI boom but also converting that growth into solid revenues and earnings growth. However, the latest controversy surrounding NVIDIA's boardroom drama and the subsequent ouster of Jensen Huang as CEO is a significant concern for investors in the future.

Story Continues

NVIDIA will lose a visionary leader, whose continuous innovation helped the company maintain a competitive position in the rapidly evolving AI market. His earlier investments in graphics processing units helped NVIDIA establish a competitive advantage against its peers. He also played a crucial role in building partnerships among major tech players, and his departure could give an undue advantage to rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. .

Moving ahead, NVIDIA's capability to sustain an extraordinary growth rate without Huang at the helm will be closely monitored, and any leadership uncertainty could dent investors' confidence. But as NVIDIA grapples with leadership succession, Cisco stands out for its stable succession planning and management continuity. The company's CEO, Chuck Robbins, has held the position since 2015 and has assured investors that in his absence, the company's strategic decisions and execution won't be hampered.

Growing concerns about the sustainability of AI spending could create additional uncertainty around NVIDIA's future growth trajectory. Cisco, on the other hand, has a diversified revenue stream, making it less dependent on the AI boom. It can benefit from broader IT spending, providing additional growth opportunities, and could offer greater resilience if AI-related spending moderates.

Cisco reported record revenues of $18.5 billion in the fiscal first quarter of 2027, up 24% year over year, according to the company's Nov. 12 press release. However, Cisco's revenue growth wasn't only dependent on AI investments by hyperscalers; it was broad-based, across various business segments like networking, cybersecurity, collaboration and software.

Additionally, similar to NVIDIA, Cisco is translating its revenue growth into stronger earnings and demonstrating operational efficiency. Its GAAP net income jumped 59% year over year to $4.6 billion in the fiscal first quarter. Furthermore, management has raised its full-year 2027 revenue guidance to $74.8-$75.8 billion and increased its earnings expectations, reflecting confidence in future business growth.

Therefore, while NVIDIA offers greater AI-driven growth potential, Cisco's management stability, diversified revenue streams, and positive outlook make it an attractive investment for investors looking for more balanced growth. news.Title: STMicroelectronics Sees Data Center Revenue More Than Doubling in 2027 as AI Demand Surges
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in STMicroelectronics N.V.? Here are five stocks we like better.

STMicroelectronics expects data center revenue to more than double to about $2.8 billion in 2027, from $1.3 billion in 2026. Silicon photonics is expected to lead growth, though manufacturing and supply-chain constraints may limit how much demand the company can fulfill.

Gross-margin improvement is expected to accelerate in the second half of 2027 as data center sales rise and factory-loading inefficiencies ease. Longer term, the company targets a 44%–46% gross margin at an $18 billion revenue run rate.

STMicroelectronics expects industrial revenue to grow by $1 billion in 2027, driven by data center power and cooling, automation, robotics and power infrastructure. Automotive growth is also expected, while personal electronics revenue is forecast to decline slightly.

STMicroelectronics Could Reach New Highs—Here's What Needs to Happen

STMicroelectronics (NYSE:STM) expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, with silicon photonics leading the increase as demand for AI infrastructure reshapes the chipmaker's business, President and CEO Jean-Marc Chery said at an event in Barcelona.

Chery said the company expects roughly $2.8 billion in data center revenue next year, up about $1.5 billion from an expected $1.3 billion in 2026. Demand is above that forecast, he said, but the company must account for manufacturing and supply-chain constraints.

Apple, Meta, and SpaceX Are Driving a Device Boom—These 3 Stocks Could Benefit

"If we can go to $3 billion, we'll go to $3 billion," Chery said. "But today, I am confident to more than double."

Silicon photonics is expected to be the largest contributor to the increase, followed by microcontrollers, an application-specific integrated circuit, electronic integrated circuits, and analog and power products, Chery said. He said the business is spread across more than 10 customers, with none accounting for more than 30% of its revenue.

Margin Improvement Expected in Second Half

Industrial Chips Are in Rally Mode—5 Ways to Play

Chery pointed to the company's fourth-quarter revenue outlook of $4.15 billion and gross margin of 39%. He said third-quarter results were slightly above guidance and that the book-to-bill ratio was well above 2.0 across all verticals, including automotive.

The CEO said data center products, including microcontrollers and photonics used around pluggable optical cables, were a significant driver of the expected fourth-quarter revenue increase. Automotive and industrial sales also contributed, he said.

Story Continues

For 2027, Chery expects gross margin in the first half to be broadly flat with the fourth-quarter level. Higher costs would be offset in part by price increases, a more favorable product mix and the gradual reduction of factory-loading inefficiencies, he said.

He expects margin improvement to accelerate in the second half as data center sales grow and the company begins to benefit from its manufacturing reshaping plan. Over time, the company's model calls for a gross margin of 44% to 46% at an $18 billion revenue run rate, with restructuring benefits progressively coming through in 2028, he said.

Chery cautioned that some planned factory closures could be delayed to accommodate customers. If customers need facilities kept open longer, he said, they should contribute to the additional costs on a nonrecurring basis.

Industrial and Automotive Growth

Chery expects industrial revenue to increase by $1 billion in 2027, citing demand from data center power and cooling infrastructure, automation, robotics and power-supply infrastructure.

In automotive, he described an industry being reshaped by electrification. Assuming high-single-digit growth for STMicroelectronics in 2027, he said roughly half would come from silicon carbide products tied to electrification, with the remainder from increased semiconductor content in legacy systems.

Automotive growth is likely to be limited in the first half by a manufacturing transition at Agrate before accelerating in the second half, Chery said.

Personal electronics, by contrast, is expected to decline slightly next year. Chery said he expects business with the company's main customer to be broadly flat and described 2027 as a transition year for the segment.

Capacity and Investment

Chery said manufacturing flexibility would be limited in 2027 as the company executes its reshaping plan. STMicroelectronics plans to expand capacity at Crolles beyond 15,000 wafers per week, potentially reaching 20,000 between 2028 and 2030, he said. Full build-out at Agrate is expected to reach 8,000 wafers per week by 2028.

The company will disclose its 2027 capital spending plans in January, Chery said. He defended investment in 300-millimeter manufacturing capacity in Europe, saying the technology can support products including silicon photonics and microcontrollers.

Research and development spending will rise as the company shifts further toward infrastructure products, Chery said, though he expects expenses to grow much more slowly than revenue. He identified optical engines, microcontrollers and low-Earth-orbit satellite communications as areas requiring continued investment.

About STMicroelectronics (NYSE:STM)

STMicroelectronics is a global semiconductor company that designs, develops and manufactures chips and related products for customers in a range of industries. Its portfolio includes microcontrollers, analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits, power semiconductors, sensors, and microelectromechanical systems (MEMS). The company's products are used in automotive systems, industrial equipment, communications devices, computers and consumer electronics. Its offerings support applications such as vehicle control and safety, factory automation, power management, and motion and environmental sensing.

news.Title: Insiders Rarely Do This. Intel’s CEO Just Bought Millions in INTC Stock After the Crash.
news.Content:
Intel (INTC) reported earnings on Oct. 29, beating its own guidance for revenue and EPS. Due to a weak outlook, however, INTC stock crashed almost 29% the next day, marking its worst day since 1974.

On Nov. 2, though, CEO Lip-Bu Tan bought 150,000 shares through his family trust at about $64.73 each. That comes out to a purchase of roughly $9.7 million. Intel stock has kept falling since, now trading at about $55 per share, more than 60% below its 52-week high of $142.35.

More News from Barchart

Dear SpaceX Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 19

Dear Nvidia Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for December 10

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 20

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

Tan also bought shares worth about $10 million in August at $95 per share, during Intel's $20 billion capital raise. In total, the CEO has put about $19.7 million into Intel since August. He is currently sitting on a loss, but because he continues to buy more, Tan seems to believe the market is wrong about Intel.

Still, a CEO buying his company's shares doesn't guarantee that the stock goes up, and this is something Intel investors have seen before. Former CEO Bob Swan once bought shares on seven different days, and INTC stock was higher a year later for six of those cases. On the other hand, former CEO Pat Gelsinger bought on 17 different days between October 2021 and November 2024, and INTC stock was lower a year later for 11 of those purchases.

While Tan's buying shows confidence, I think the direction of Intel stock will come down to whether the company can fix its supply problems and deliver. Let's take a closer look.

About Intel Stock

Intel designs and makes the processors that power PCs and data-center servers, while the company is also building a foundry business to manufacture chips for other companies. Since taking over as CEO, Tan has focused on fixing Intel's manufacturing and keeping up with surging demand for its Xeon server chips. Founded in 1968, Intel is headquartered in Santa Clara, California.

So far this year, INTC stock has climbed about 48%, outperforming the VanEck Semiconductor ETF's (SMH) 28% gain during the same period. Most of Intel stock's surge came in the first half of 2026, though, with shares down 49% for the past six months. INTC stock has kept falling since its third-quarter report and is down about 39% for the past month alone.

Intel stock looks somewhat cheap on earnings but expensive on sales. The forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 53.4 times sits below its five-year average of about 63 times, but that average is inflated by years when Intel barely earned anything. In contrast, the price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 5.5 times is above the average of 3.2 times, which shows that investors are still paying up for the turnaround.

Story Continues

The EPS outlook helps justify the high P/S multiple. Analysts expect earnings to jump exponentially in fiscal 2026, partly due to profits recovering from a very low base, before growing 26% year-over-year (YOY) in fiscal 2027. The balance sheet is strong as well, with about $54 billion in cash and short-term investments against roughly $50.1 billion in debt.

Overall, if Intel can find a way to fix its supply problems, I think Tan's stock purchases could prove well-timed.

Strong Quarter, Weak Outlook

Intel reported Q3 2026 results on Oct. 29. Revenue rose 21% YOY to $16.5 billion, while adjusted EPS of $0.52 came in well above the roughly $0.40 analysts expected. The data-center business grew 78%, its fastest growth in 15 years. The period was the 8th consecutive quarter that Intel beat its own guidance, and CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the priority will be to increase supply to meet strong demand for its Xeon chips.

What hurt INTC stock was the outlook. Intel guided Q4 revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $17.1 billion Wall Street expected. Management also expects PC chip revenue to fall more than 20% from Q3. A shutdown at a factory in Israel is expected to cost about $600 million in revenue across Q4 2026 and Q1 2027.

What Do Analysts Expect for Intel Stock?

Based on 46 Wall Street analysts with coverage, Intel stock has a consensus "Hold" rating. The mean price target of $92.67 indicates potential upside of 70% from current levels. Although the majority of analysts rate INTC stock as a "Hold," Intel's recent sharp selloff means that even the lowest price target of $63 now sits above the current share price.

news.Title: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
news.Content:
By Che Pan and Wen-Yee Lee

Nov 19 (Reuters) - Taiwan's TSMC is tightening restrictions on Chinese chip designers, suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders and generally limiting affected customers to older chipmaking ‌technology, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The move could close one of the last ‌remaining routes for Chinese companies to produce powerful AI processors, complicating Beijing's efforts to develop domestic alternatives to chips designed by Nvidia ​and manufactured by TSMC.

The world's largest contract chipmaker has instructed that affected orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below be halted unless customers obtain US export licences, the people said.

Chinese designers will generally be limited to older 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided their chips do not use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) or require advanced packaging, according to TSMC ‌guidance reviewed by the two people.

Most ⁠leading AI chips are produced using 7-nanometre processes or smaller, enabling faster and more energy-efficient performance. HBM allows processors to handle the vast data volumes required by AI applications, ⁠while advanced packaging integrates chips and memory to boost computing power.

US CLOSES MANUFACTURING ROUTE

The restrictions follow new US Commerce Department rules that took effect on Thursday, removing a compliance route that had allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced manufacturing ​services ​without individual export licences.

Previously, TSMC could check the computing power ​and other technical characteristics of certain Chinese ‌chip designs to determine whether they fell outside US export controls.

Under the new rules, TSMC can no longer use that verification process for affected Chinese customers. Their advanced chips are instead presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless an exception applies.

The Financial Times first reported on Thursday that TSMC and South Korea's Samsung Electronics had suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following the new restrictions.

CHINA'S AI CHIP AMBITIONS

The measures ‌could particularly affect Chinese companies developing alternatives to Nvidia's processors, ​including independent chip designers and technology giants that have developed in-house ​chips.

A US government list of approved chip designers ​includes Nvidia, AMD, Apple and Taiwanese companies MediaTek and Realtek, but no mainland Chinese ‌firms.

Some Chinese AI chip designers still had access ​to TSMC's 7-nanometre manufacturing technology ​before Thursday, a separate source with direct knowledge of the matter said. Reuters could not independently verify the arrangements under which those chips were manufactured.

Story Continues

TSMC's guidance also requires closer scrutiny of customers' operating locations, ​parent companies, major shareholders, packaging providers ‌and shipping routes, the people said.

The checks extend to orders placed through overseas subsidiaries or ​intermediaries, including entities in Taiwan, the US, Europe, Japan and Southeast Asia.

(Reporting by Pan Che and ​Wen-Yee Lee. Editing by Eduardo Baptista and Mark Potter)
